10688-the-camp-fire-girls-at-camp-keeway:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls at Camp Keewaydin for girls who loved camp stories, sending seventy-five girls by steamer to a summer camp. The book opens in a rush at the dock, where Captain MacLaren's boat, the Carribou, waits while girls such as Hinpoha and Agony scramble with suitcases down the hill. Camp life, friendship, and outdoor fun follow.

Frey mixes humor with the Camp Fire ideals of work, health, and loyalty, as the girls paddle, hike, and settle camp quarrels. The tone is cheerful and wholesome, aimed at young readers of its day. Modern readers get a lively period piece about girls' camping in early twentieth-century America.
10892-dawn: A novel by H. Rider Haggard, published in 1884 in seventy-six chapters. Haggard, later famous for adventure romances of Africa and lost worlds, writes here at the start of his career, in the long Victorian novel form. The book's scale alone marks it as an ambitious early work, told across a wide cast and many scenes.
11875-the-blood-red-dawn:
Charles Caldwell Dobie's 1920 novel The Blood Red Dawn opens with a pastor's announcement lost in a hum of inattention. Claire Robson leans toward her mother and asks whether she caught the speaker's name. Her mother dismisses him as a foreigner of some sort, setting up a story of social judgment and attraction.

Later scenes follow Claire through dances, embarrassment before admirers such as Stillman, and arguments with a man named Flint, who insists she stay where she is and enjoy the meal. Dobie uses drawing-room encounters, dances, and family talk to explore how a young woman navigates desire, reputation, and the expectations of those around her.
14096-with-links-of-steel-or-the-peril-o:
Nicholas Carter's 1904 Nick Carter tale sends the famous detective after the Kilgore diamond gang. A crafty robbery opens the case, and a trail of clues leads through Señora Cervera's circle to a dead body and a startling find. Carter questions witnesses, follows suspects through New York streets, and pieces together how the gang moves its loot. Each chapter ends with a fresh turn.

Science sharpens the mystery. A long passage explains how heat and pressure turn carbon into diamond, and how makers chase artificial stones. Carter uses that knowledge to test what the gang claims and what it hides. Pulp energy drives the prose: short scenes, quick dialogue, and a hero who stays cool under threat. Fans of early detective fiction will enjoy the mix of street work, lab talk, and steady pursuit.
15053-the-evolution-of-an-english-town:
Gordon Home tells the evolution of an English town, Pickering in Yorkshire, from prehistoric times up to 1905. A preface, list of illustrations and a chapter concerning those which follow open the book, with a section of Fork Cottage among its plates.

Forest and vale of Pickering in Palaeolithic and pre-glacial times follow, with later chapters tracing settlement, church, castle, market and modern town through fourteen chapters and more. Home writes local history as evolution: landscape, people and buildings changing together. The volume suits readers of Yorkshire history and of how one town grew from forest clearing to market centre.
15778-the-honorable-miss-a-story-of-an-o:
A girls' story by L. T. Meade, author of A World of Girls and Sweet Girl Graduate. Hurst and Company issued it in New York as part of Meade's uniform series. The Honorable Miss lives in an old-fashioned town, where manners, duty, and reputation rule. Meade writes for girls who liked tales of school, home, and plucky heroines.

The heroine, a young lady of rank and spirit, faces town gossip, family duty, and the claims of love. Old-fashioned ways both shelter and confine her. Meade keeps the plot busy with balls, quarrels, and kind deeds. The book charms as a period girls' tale: proper on the surface, spirited underneath, and firm that honour means more than rank.
15964-the-child-of-the-dawn:
A visionary novel by Arthur Christopher Benson, Fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, issued in 1912. Benson, author of The Upton Letters and From a College Window, dedicates the book to his best and dearest friend Herbert Francis William Tatham. The narrator wakes from an operation in deadly sickness and ghastly confusion, at the end of a worn-out material life. Dawn breaks on another kind of life.

The child of the dawn learns a world beyond the body, where hope replaces fear. Benson writes with quiet, scholarly grace, mixing philosophy with fable. The tale moves slowly, by talk and vision, not by plot. It appeals to readers who ask what lies past death: a gentle, hopeful dream of a new morning.
16991-the-circus-comes-to-town:
Lebbeus Mitchell's 1921 boys' book follows Jerry Elbow, a small-town boy with big circus dreams. A gifted apple, a black half-dollar, and a green elephant lead him toward tickets to paradise. Chapters on clowns, crocodile tears, and a dizzy seat of glory fill the road to show day. Gary, Celia Jane, and a chalk-faced clown share the fun.

The tale is told with humor and a soft heart for kids who scheme, save, and blunder toward a wish. Its circus scenes feel lived in, from lanes of crying children to rides on elephants. Young readers who love circuses and scrappy heroes will find this a cheerful, old-style treat.
17263-the-astonishing-history-of-troy-to:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch's Astonishing History of Troy Town, in its 1914 reprint of the 1888 tale, opens with a dedication to Charles Cannan. It begins with a joke about a pedagogue thanked for a ticket-of-leave. Chapters promise an admiral who mistakes one gentleman for another, and a blue-jerseyed man who hoists no more bricks. Twin brothers, lepers, a lady with a musical voice used to deceive, and a crew shipwrecked on washing day follow.

Quiller-Couch writes in witty, Cornish-flavored prose, with tall tales and sly asides at every turn. The town of Troy, its sailors, and its eccentrics make a comic world all their own. Readers who like Dickensian humor and seaside farce will enjoy a bright, old-style novel of a small town gone wonderfully astray.
17784-the-story-of-bawn:
Katharine Tynan wrote The Story of Bawn, printed in Chicago in 1907 by A. C. McClurg. Bawn, an Irish girl, tells her own tale, from her youth and home ghosts to the creamery, a nurse, and a rough lover who tests her heart.

Chapters move through a stile in the wood, a trap, a friend, an enemy, a miniature, and an empty house, as Bawn learns who she can trust. Tynan, famed for Irish tales, writes with warmth for country life and Catholic feeling. It is a gentle, old Irish romance, best for readers who like a heroine who grows wise through trial.
18621-the-story-of-cooperstown:
Ralph Birdsall, rector of Christ Church, published this history of Cooperstown at New York in 1925 with Scribner's, after a first printing in 1917. Sixty-eight photographs aid the tale, from Council Rock and Otsego Lake to the Leatherstocking Monument and Hyde Hall. Chapters open with the Indians and the coming of white men, then a bypath of the Revolution and the start of settlement.

Later chapters cover old homes and gossip, the pioneer courtroom, Father Nash, Natty Bumppo, gallows tales, the birthplace of baseball, and Fenimore Cooper in the village. A village map and guide close the book. Birdsall writes with local pride and a storyteller's ease.
18668-in-search-of-the-unknown:
Robert W. Chambers published this book at New York and London in 1904 with Harper and Brothers. Its narrator quits a government post on February 29 and takes work under Professor Farrago as head of the waterfowl section of a new zoological garden at Bronx Park. Within a month he sees things he can scarcely credit, from a stealthy purring undertow to sights he fears he will soon disbelieve.

Chambers frames the tales as true records told simply, with friends to vouch for the teller. Nature study, odd beasts, and a creeping sense of the uncanny mix through the book. It is an early blend of natural history romance and weird fiction from a popular writer of the day.
204-the-innocence-of-father-brown:
A small Catholic priest with a round face solves crimes by understanding sinners. G. K. Chesterton's Innocence of Father Brown gathers twelve stories, from The Blue Cross to The Three Tools of Death. Flambeau the thief, Valentin the detective, and quiet English villages recur.

Father Brown sees what clever men miss because he knows how ordinary people think and fail. The Secret Garden, The Queer Feet, and The Hammer of God show his method at its best. Chesterton mixes paradox, humor, and moral insight in each tale. The collection founded the clerical detective story.
21310-featherland-how-the-birds-lived-at:
George Manville Fenn wrote this bird book for two little girls who leaned against his knee asking for stories. Greenlawn's garden birds become characters: Flutethroat the blackbird, grumpy at being called Yellowbill, and Spottleover the thrush among them. The dog, cat, bees, hedgehog, flies, and wasps join the company.

Fenn, a serious naturalist, watches how the birds actually behave toward each other. He gives them only small snatches of speech to make their actions plain. Even a skylark's song and a bluebottle's hum find places. The language stays easy for young children, with an odd hard word slipped in. It is nature study disguised as garden gossip.
21550-the-king-s-own:
The Mutiny at the Nore in 1797 opens Captain Marryat's The King's Own, published in 1830 as his second book. Few events, Marryat says, caused more alarm at the time or more interest since. He wrote much of it while still at sea.

His ship was then hunting a reported island in mid-Atlantic that did not exist. Out of those slow watches came a polished tale of naval life and revolt. Marryat's gift for inventing episodes shows already in full force. The book helped prove that a serving sailor could write fiction to match any landsman.
21650-london-town:
Felix Leigh versifies, and Thomas Crane and Ellen Houghton picture, London Town for young readers. Verses invite children, great and small, to climb St Paul's with the book in hand. From the dome they look down over the busy hive of London.

Pages treat the Houses of Parliament, the Tower, the omnibus, and the penny-ice man. The Tower was a prison of old, where few who entered came out. Now children may visit any day without fear or doubt. Covent Garden, the orange girl, and the first of May fill a gay, rhyming tour of the Victorian city.
21659-some-everyday-folk-and-dawn:
Miles Franklin sets Some Everyday Folk and Dawn in the small town of Noonoon, first published in 1909. A big swell of a driver grunts up to a box seat as the tale begins. The narrator rides in the body of the cart, studying his coloured neck.

Franklin inscribes the book to English men who believe in votes for women. Australian women, she notes, won their rights as voters in 1902 without forced suffrage fights. Grandma Clay's love story, Dawn's ambition, and Miss Flipp fill the chapters. Provincial politics and dentists get satiric turns in a tale both funny and pointed.
22214-molly-bawn:
Margaret Wolfe Hamilton, who wrote as "The Duchess," published Molly Bawn in 1878. It was her breakthrough novel, and its name became a byword. Molly is a bright, reckless Irish girl visiting an English country house. Mr. Massereene, watching his wife's dejection, wishes aloud that he knew what to do about a guest who may or may not come.

Around Molly the house party talks, flirts, and misunderstands at speed. The Duchess writes dialogue like drawing-room firework displays. Beneath the sparkle sits a real question about Molly's honour and her future. The novel sold in huge numbers and made Irish charm a fashion in Victorian fiction.
223-the-wisdom-of-father-brown:
Father Brown returns in a second set of twelve mysteries, wiser and no less paradoxical. G. K. Chesterton's Wisdom of Father Brown opens with The Absence of Mr Glass and runs through thieves, duels, and a salad that hides murder. Dr. Orion Hood, a criminologist, provides a foil.

The priest solves crimes by thinking like the criminal, not by footprints or science. The Paradise of Thieves, The Head of Caesar, and The God of the Gongs show his range. Chesterton's humor and theology color every solution. The collection deepens the priest-detective's fame.
23181-thomas-jefferson-brown: James Oliver Curwood's Thomas Jefferson Brown turns on a doctor's blunt advice. The man is told that, if he wants to live long enough to see grandchildren, he should tramp for a while: live outdoors, sleep outdoors, breathe fresh air, and walk. Curwood calls that doctor Fate at work, playing its game from behind spectacles and a broad, bumpy forehead.
23278-janice-day-at-poketown:
Helen Beecher Long's Janice Day at Poketown, from 1914, opens with a journey's last leg. An officious man in a blue cap on the dock shouts the call to board the moment passengers step down from the little narrow-gauge train. Janice has been riding those cars for more than two hours.

Even so, it is some minutes before the wheezy old steamer gets under way. Long savours the small delays of rural travel: caps, calls, and a boat in no hurry. Readers get a girls' novel of a small town, reached slowly, where Janice's stay at Poketown can begin.
24011-zodiac-town:
Nancy Byrd Turner published Zodiac Town, The Rhymes of Amos and Ann, in Boston in 1921, illustrated by Winifred Bromhall. Turner acknowledges permission to reprint verses that had appeared in The Youth's Companion, St. Nicholas, and other periodicals, and dedicates the book to her father.

The contents are a calendar in rhyme: Zodiac Town itself, then January through December, one chapter for each month. Amos and Ann, pictured on the frontispiece with the journeying man, walk children through the year's signs and seasons. For young readers, it is a gentle introduction to the zodiac, told in verses meant to be read aloud and remembered.
2513-god-the-known-and-god-the-unknown:
Samuel Butler first published these essays as articles in the Examiner in the spring and summer of 1879, then revised them for book form. They belong with his earlier works on habit and evolution, and they carry his argument that living things, from plants to people, show purpose in how they grow and act.

Butler draws a line between the God we can know through the world around us and a God beyond all knowing. He writes in plain, combative prose, using homely examples from plants, animals, and daily life. Readers get a sharp Victorian challenge to both church dogma and cold mechanism, and a view of faith rooted in life itself.
25283-explorers-of-the-dawn:
Mazo de la Roche's Explorers of the Dawn, published by Knopf in 1922 with a foreword by Christopher Morley, follows three children at the dawn of their lives. The narrator and Angel take lessons under a strict governess, Mrs. Handsomebody, while baby Seraph toddles at the edge of their world.

A telegram bursts into the schoolroom while the children stumble over the Channel Islands, darkening the day. Mary Ellen the maid brings it with apologies, and the governess restores cold order. De la Roche writes of childhood adventure, scolding, and tenderness with humor and a keen ear for children's talk.
2550-tales-of-trail-and-town:
Bret Harte sets these stories in the rough camps of the gold country, where a new hotel, a gin mill, and a disputed town name mark the march of so called progress. Peter Atherly's ancestors, two Americans abroad in spirit, and Alkali Dick each take a turn in the spotlight.

Judgment falls on Bolinas Plain, a night on the Divide tests hard men, and the youngest prospector in Calaveras learns his trade. Harte writes with irony about towns that polish their past as fast as they mine it. The tales reward readers who like frontier comedy edged with a sting.
25534-little-folks-a-magazine-for-the-yo:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young from Cassell and Company, gathers stories, pictures, and verses for child readers in this enlarged series volume. The transcriber notes the scans give no firm date, though the project listed it as an August 1884 edition.

One serial, A Little Too Clever, by the author of Pen's Perplexities, follows Elsie and Duncan, with Elsie resolved to go while the weather holds. Such serials, mixed with shorter pieces, made Little Folks a regular fireside companion for Victorian children and their families. Cassell issued the magazine in London, Paris, and New York.
26034-grey-town:
Gerald R. Baldwin sets an Australian story of a priest, a town, and a stubborn silence in Grey Town, printed at Melbourne in 1922. Contents run from the presbytery and Michael O'Connor to the Quirks, promotion, Denis Quirk, readjustment, and the death of the Observer. Days of storm and stress, rumor hydra headed, temptation, Sylvia Jackson, and Denis refusing to speak follow, with Father Healy's mission and a gorge crossing.

A frontispiece shows a woman raising an oar and bringing it down smartly across a man's knuckles. One scene finds a priest's sister vowing to check herself lest she chase the postman through town with a pitchfork, while Mrs. Quirk urges prayer and returning good for evil. Baldwin writes of small town pride, faith, and talk with warmth and bite.
26207-in-our-town:
William Allen White's 1906 volume gathers nineteen stories about a Kansas town and its people. Contents list scribes and Pharisees, a young prince, a society editor, the coming of the leisure class, and the Bolton girl's position. Other tales treat a loathed but esteemed rival paper, the casting out of Jimmy Myers, and the passing of Priscilla Winthrop.

Illustrations catch small-town types at their desks, parties, and street corners. One shows a man whose collars stand so high he orders them from a drummer. White writes with warmth and satire, praising neighbourly decency while poking fun at pride, gossip, and new wealth. The book gives a lively portrait of Midwestern town life in his day.
26256-a-little-maid-of-province-town:
Alice Turner Curtis's 1913 children's book, one of her Little Maid series, follows Anne Nelson of Province Town. Anne arrives at Mistress Stoddard's door, sent by a wharf man's word that the house holds no little girls. Captain Enos at first refuses her a roof, then leads her in tenderly, to Mrs. Stoddard's relief.

Chapters promise Anne's secret, a wolf, scarlet stockings, capture by Indians, a voyage out to sea, and life as castaways on an island. Later come Captain Enos's secrets, an unexpected journey, and Anne finding her father. A candy party, a spring picnic, and the sloop Peggy close the tale. The book mixes colonial adventure with a child's search for home.
26431-children-of-our-town:
Pictured by E. Mars and M. H. Squire, with verses by Carolyn Wells, this 1902 picture book shows city children at play. Boys fly kites on a blustering windy day, sail boats on a lake until the wind upsets them, and ride the goat-carriage along the Mall in Central Park. A proud Belinda, dressed in Sunday best at Coney Island, cannot comfortably dig in the sand.

Each picture carries a short, teasing verse, often warning aged duffers and grandsires not to try the children's games themselves. Old men are told not to fly large kites or splash about sailing boats, and grandams learn to swap velvet and nets for simple gingham at the shore. The book is a light, affectionate portrait of New York childhood.
26992-the-wind-before-the-dawn:
Dell H. Munger's 1912 novel follows Elizabeth, a woman caught between a husband, a home, and a wider life she can see but not yet reach. Chapters carry her from castles in Spain and a trip to Topeka through cyclones, mortgages of soul, and a marriage sermon on wives submitting to husbands.

Elizabeth weighs domestic duty against social ideals, her wages counted as food and clothing, her judgment tested at every turn. The novel reads as an early feminist story of the prairie, sympathetic to a woman who refuses to settle for the life handed to her.
27066-making-a-lawn:
Luke J. Doogue's Making a Lawn, published in 1912 in the House and Garden Making Books, teaches the home-maker how to build and keep a lawn. Doogue, superintendent of Boston's public grounds, calls the lawn the most important element in the setting of most country houses.

The handbook covers the small lawn old and new, the treatment of large areas, and grass seed in detail, naming creeping bent, Rhode Island bent for putting greens, and crested dog's-tail. Pictures and diagrams show how to bind banks, level ground, and keep grass thriving through the seasons.
27404-where-the-strange-trails-go-down:
E. Alexander Powell, author of Fighting in Flanders and Italy at War, published this travel book with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in October 1921, with illustrations and a map. Its subtitle lists the ground covered: Sulu, Borneo, Celebes, Bali, Java, Sumatra, the Straits Settlements, the Malay States, Siam, Cambodia, Annam, and Cochin-China.

Powell cruised more than six thousand miles aboard the coastguard cutter Negros, placed at his disposal through the courtesy of Philippine officials. He dedicates the book to Margaret Campbell McCutchen, who kept smiling through countless discomforts. A Dyak head-hunter with a sumpitan blow-gun fronts the volume. It is a vivid tour of Southeast Asia's frontiers.
27651-the-two-hundredth-anniversary-of-t:
Daniel Davenport of Bridgeport, Connecticut, delivered this address at New Milford on June 17, 1907, marking two hundred years since the town's settlement began in 1707. The speech looks back to a time when northwestern Connecticut was still frontier wilderness, thirty miles from Long Island Sound.

Davenport traces how settlers pushed inland from older coastal towns such as Milford and Stratford, and how farming methods of the day made even settled districts feel crowded. The address honors the town's founders while giving listeners a plain account of colonial growth, hardship, and the slow clearing of the forest frontier.
27716-a-portrait-of-old-george-town:
Grace Dunlop Ecker wrote this portrait of old Georgetown, published in Richmond, Virginia, in 1951 in a revised and enlarged second edition. Ecker, born in the town, says plainly that she does not mean to write a history, but to paint a portrait of the place she loves.

The book opens with a poem on Georgetown ghosts recalling the days when the Federal City was its guest, then moves through families, streets, and houses. It preserves the memory of a once-independent seaport town that was gradually absorbed into Washington. Ecker dedicated the book to her father and mother and her aunt, all of whom lived long and useful lives in Georgetown.
28448-the-campfire-girls-of-roselawn:
Margaret Penrose's The Campfire Girls of Roselawn, subtitled A Strange Message from the Air, catches the early radio craze through a group of American schoolgirls. The story opens when Jessie Norwood insists that radio, the wireless telephone, is the newest wonder. Her friends then begin stringing aerials to hear voices from the air.

Chapters follow a canoe trip, a bazaar, a Fourth of July celebration, and a puzzling broadcast that turns into a mystery of the ether. Penrose mixes campfire friendship, jokes, and practical detail about receiving sets. Modern readers get a lively picture of how thrilling radio seemed when it first entered ordinary homes.
28695-our-children-scenes-from-the-count:
Anatole France wrote a set of short scenes about children, illustrated in color and pen and ink by Boutet de Monvel. The American edition, published by Duffield in 1923 from a 1917 copyright, follows Fanny on a visit to her grandmother, a fancy dress party, a school, pan-pipes, Roger's stable, and Catherine's day. Each piece is brief, like a sketch from a child's day in country or town.

France, better known for novels and satire, writes here with tenderness and light humor, watching children without preaching at them. The pictures share the honors with the text, giving the book the feel of a gift volume. Readers get a charming set of glimpses into French childhood as an old master imagined it, gentle, observant, and free of sentimentality.
28727-a-boy-s-town:
W. D. Howells's A Boy's Town, described for Harper's Young People and published by Harper and Brothers in 1890, recalls boyhood in a town. Howells, author of The Shadow of a Dream, April Hopes, and A Hazard of New Fortunes, writes for young readers rather than critics. An illustration shows a visitor coming up to the author's boy where he sat fishing.

The volume belongs to a boy's-eye view of town life: its streets, neighbors, games, and small adventures, told in the plain style Howells used for young people. Other Howells books listed beside it range from novels to farces and travel sketches. Readers get an American boyhood remembered by a novelist, gentle, observant, and made for family reading.
28906-the-tale-of-timber-town:
A. A. Grace wrote this 1914 novel, The Tale of Timber Town, published by Gordon and Gotch across Australia and New Zealand. Grace, author of Tales of a Dying Race and Folk-Tales of the Maori, sets his story in a gold and timber town. Chapters open with a master goldsmith, the wreck of the Mersey Witch, and the pilot's daughter, then bring Rachel Varnhagen, Bill the prospector, and the father of Timber Town.

Later chapters follow cut-throat euchre, the yellow flag, a robbery of the mails, and the gold league, through digging, a den of thieves, and gold and roses. The goldsmith comes to town three times, and Benjamin finds redemption. Readers get a lively Australasian tale of gold, rogues, and romance, told with local color and a busy plot.
29193-dream-town:
Henry Slesar wrote this short science fiction story about a strange little town a traveler might blunder into on a rainy evening. Sol Becker, his car stolen by a hitchhiker, seeks a room for the night from a plump, apple-cheeked woman in a nightgown and house-robe. She seems harmless, like a mother from a political cartoon.

Slesar warns the reader to beware the Knights, the town's hidden power, and the harmless doorway soon turns sinister. The story plays on small-town welcome curdling into menace. Readers get a compact tale of a traveler trapped by politeness, where every kindly face may hide a threat.
2949-stories-of-a-western-town:
Octave Thanet, the pen name of Alice French, collected five stories of an Iowa town in Stories of a Western Town. The contents include The Besetment of Kurt Lieders, The Face of Failure, Tommy and Thomas, Mother Emeritus, and Harry Lossing. The first story opens on a December morning at six, with silver rime down a wooden sidewalk and dead leaves on macadam and stiff mud.

Thanet's town is low, wooden, and well kept, its houses gay with geraniums despite the sharp wind. Characters face failure, debt, and neighborly judgment, while a smile from Miss Brown softens the face of failure itself. The stories give a sympathetic, unsentimental picture of Midwestern life, written by an author who knew its small towns from inside.
29561-in-a-little-town:
Rupert Hughes's In a Little Town, printed in 1917 by Harper and Brothers of New York and London, gathers stories of small-town American life. Its contents run from Don't You Care and Pop through Baby Talk, The Mouth of the Gift Horse, and The Old Folks at Home. A character named Govers hopes a girl will be awful pretty, and asks for a glimpse of her, claiming a right to see.

Hughes writes with warmth and humor about neighbors, babies, and the talk of a town where everyone knows everyone. The book stands beside his Thirteenth Commandment and Clipped Wings in the same list. Readers of American short stories will find a fond, funny portrait of town life a century ago.
29936-flamedown:
H. B. Fyfe wrote Flamedown for Analog Science Fact and Fiction in August 1961, with pictures by Summers. Its headnote calls the tale, of course, one hell of an ending for a trip to Mars. Amid sounds of rending and shattering that linger dimly, Charlie Holmes slips from reality as blackness sweeps over him in a wave of agony.

He turns his head gently a few inches to the right, then to the left, and, finding the pain far less than he feared, he opens his eyes. A bulbous creature squats beside his pallet and rasps Hel-lo. Charlie shuts his eyes tight, then feels a damp, spongy tip, likely one of the grape-red tentacles he glimpsed, prod his shoulder. Hel-lo insists the scratchy voice, and Charlie, trapped peeping, opens his eyes resignedly to ask where in hell he is.
30148-the-house-in-town:
Susan Warner continues her series with the third novel, a sequel to Opportunities, in which Matilda moves from country life to a house in town. The opening finds her rushing to tell Norton her news, only to wait while he digs at a shoemaker's fault in his boot with penknife and file. That mix of eager youth and patient waiting sets the tone for a tale of town manners, household duty, and growing faith.

Robert Carter and Brothers published the New York volume in 1872, entering it in 1871, with an epistle text on the title page about a soldier who avoids the affairs of life. Warner, author of The Wide Wide World, keeps the focus on home, friendship, and moral choice. Readers of the earlier books will find Matilda older, sharper, and still learning what she can do.
3031-wild-animals-i-have-known:
Ernest Thompson Seton wrote Wild Animals I Have Known as true stories of animals he had watched, insisting the creatures were real characters who lived the lives depicted. The contents include Lobo, king of Currumpaw, and Silverspot the crow. Raggylug the cottontail rabbit, Bingo the dog, the Springfield fox, the pacing mustang, Wully the yellow dog, and Redruff the Don Valley partridge follow. Seton admits leaving the strict line of historical truth in places, yet claims the animals showed heroism and personality more strongly than his pages can show.

A cottontail scene has a mother rabbit still in death while her son Rag leads a fox away with a barbed-wire trick. The book founded modern animal biography, treating wild lives with respect and drama.
30546-george-brown:
John Lewis writes George Brown for The Makers of Canada series, edited by Duncan Campbell Scott, Pelham Edgar, and William Dawson Le Sueur. Published in Toronto in 1906 as an edition de luxe, this copy is number eighty-eight of four hundred signed and numbered sets.

Contents open with a chapter titled From Scotland to Canada, tracing Brown's move from his Scottish roots to a Canadian career. Brown stands among the makers of Canada, a reformer, journalist, and public figure whose life shaped a young nation. Lewis tells that story in a scholarly yet readable biography, with portrait and notes.
31371-the-little-clown:
Thomas Cobb's 1901 children's story, published by Grant Richards in London, follows Jimmy, nearly eight, whose full name is James Orchardson Sinclair Wilmot. At Miss Lawson's small school at Ramsgate since he was six, among five other boys, Jimmy learns the school will close early when Miss Lawson falls ill. Her sister Miss Rosina sends everyone home on Tuesday, though Jimmy has no home to go to.

He has never seen his father or mother, nor his sister Winnie, born in the West Indies, and his parents left England when he was two and never returned. Thirteen chapters carry him to London, to Aunt Selina's, to a railway station, into custody, running away, to the circus, on the road, and sleeping in a windmill. Tender and adventurous, the book is a classic runaway tale.
3239-the-puppet-crown:
Harold MacGrath dedicates this romance to the memory of his father, friend and comrade of his youth. The contents promise a scepter which was a stick, the coup d'état of cousin Josef, and an episode ten years after. An adventure with royalty, a scene behind the puppet booth, and a mademoiselle of the veil follow, with a red chateau and a house party.

The puppet crown of the title is a throne worked by hidden hands. MacGrath, a master of the Ruritanian romance, sets his tale in an imaginary kingdom where plots wear evening dress. Readers who enjoy lost crowns, secret passages, and love against court intrigue will find the book's pleasures familiar and briskly served.
32462-warrior-of-the-dawn:
Howard Browne's serial, printed in Amazing Stories in December 1942 and January 1943, follows Tharn, a Cro-Magnon warrior seeking vengeance from the forest deeps. Chapter one, In Quest of Vengeance, opens late one hot afternoon on a grassland where Neela, a zebra, grazes with a family of fifteen. Neela grows nervous, lifting his head to stare east across wind-stirred grass, starting, stamping, snorting, and wheeling back.

Two hundred yards east, three half-naked white hunters lie belly-flat in concealing growth, advancing with caution. Browne sets a prehistoric world of herds, hunters, and forest killers, where Tharn's vow drives the action. An illustration shows Tharn staring in amazement at a city before him, hinting at wonders beyond the hunt. The story suits readers who enjoy lost-world adventure and stone-age heroes.
32648-the-minute-boys-of-york-town:
James Otis tells a boys' tale set in Virginia in 1781, near the close of the war with Britain. Two young Virginians watch raids by British horse, help neighbors in trouble, and get drawn into the fight around York Town.

In eighteen chapters the boys face a spy, a prisoner held in secret, and a missing friend. They also face a siege that tests their nerve and their loyalty. The story mixes camp talk, quick escapes, and hard choices, and it ends with the American guns closing in on the town.
3533-sunshine-sketches-of-a-little-town:
Stephen Leacock writes comic sketches about Mariposa, a fictional small town in Missinaba County, Ontario. The chapters follow Mr Smith's hostelry, the speculations of Jefferson Thorpe, and a Knights of Pythias marine excursion. They also cover the Reverend Mr Drone, a whirlwind election campaign, a bank mystery, and the love of Zena Pepperleigh and Peter Pupkin. Leacock, who taught at Upper Canada College and the University of Toronto, knew town life well.

Mariposa's people take themselves very seriously, which is the source of the humor. A hotel keeper, a barber, a banker, and a minister all believe their small deeds are great events. The book suits readers who enjoy gentle satire of small town Canada and a classic of Canadian humor.
35359-jimmie-moore-of-bucktown:
Melvin E Trotter wrote this mission tale, printed by the Winona Publishing Company of Chicago in 1904. A boy of ten or twelve walks into a mission and asks, in street dialect, where the boss of the place is. The superintendent turns and sees a face once seen, never forgotten: hollow cheeks, a pinched nose, and deep gray eyes at once pleading and defiant.

The boy is Jimmie Moore of Bucktown, a bread winner with burdens too heavy for his years. Chapters run through a busted funeral, Jimmie's new pa, Mrs Cook's first prayer, and Fagin's meeting. Bill's pension, a picnic, and Dave striking his gait fill the close. Trotter writes of rescue work among the poor, in the voice of the streets Jimmie came from.
35493-the-black-fawn:
Jim Kjelgaard tells a boy-and-deer story in a novel issued in New York in 1958. Bud Sloan, who is also called Allan, sits at a small kitchen table with Gram Bennett and repeats a private rule to himself. He must not let them know he is afraid, and he must remember his manners.

Inside, Bud hides his feelings with care, since showing weakness invites others to pounce on it. The Bennett household, once full of eleven children, now holds only three at most meals. The title points to the wild creature at the heart of the tale. Young readers get a tender story of an unsure boy, a farm home, and the trust that grows between people and a fawn.
35819-lonesome-town:
Ethel and James Dorrance wrote this western novel, printed by the Macaulay Company of New York with a 1922 copyright. G W Gage drew the front plate, showing a woman with a raised crop over a man who drops a bridle rein. The pair had written Glory Rides the Range and Get Your Man. They give the book to Father Knickerbocker, for the heritage of Central Park.

Chapters run from Some Place Like Home through The Sky Sign, The Old Park Lady, and Poplars Four. A man in a white sombrero, wiping his brow with a purple bandanna, fills the sample scene. Credit plans, limits of trust, and beef on the hoof mix city and range in the plot's long list of turns.
36409-harry-watson-s-high-school-days-or:
Harry Watson's High School Days, or The Rivals of Rivertown is a boys' school novel by Frank V Webster, published in New York by Cupples and Leon in 1912. Webster wrote a shelf of such books: Only a Farm Boy, Airship Andy, and The Boys of Bellwood School among them. The frontispiece shows a new student borne aloft by his schoolmates.

The publisher lists some twenty Webster titles at the front, each in cloth at a set price. Tom the Telephone Boy, Bob the Castaway, and the Young Firemen of Lakeville fill the catalogue. Harry Watson's volume sends its hero into high school rivalry in the town of Rivertown. Sports, pranks, and competing cliques drive the plot. Webster, a house name for the Stratemeyer syndicate's style of production, delivered clean adventure at factory pace for boys of the nineteen tens.
36511-the-weight-of-the-crown:
The Weight of the Crown is a novel by Fred White, copyrighted in 1904 and issued at New York and London in 1906 with illustrations. White had written Tregarthen's Wife, The Robe of Lucifer, and The Crimson Blind, named on the title page. A pictured line shows a woman saying she was going to have a look at the pictures. The contents open with a chapter called Without a Friend.

A desperate next step follows as the second chapter begins, in the brisk manner of White's tales. White was one of the most prolific English tale writers of his age, turning out romances of courts, crime, and hidden identity by the score. A crown's weight, in his hands, means the burden and danger laid on those who wear or serve one. The tale moves in his swift, scene by scene way.
36744-peggy-owen-at-yorktown:
Lucy Foster Madison wrote a novel for young readers about Peggy Owen, a Quaker girl in the American Revolution. Madison had already written three earlier Peggy Owen books. The story opens in Philadelphia on a bright winter day in February 1781, with Peggy lugging a huge bundle up Chestnut Street.

Chapter titles promise a visit to the home of Washington, the appearance of the enemy, and a journey toward Yorktown. Pictures show Peggy meeting John Paul Jones and Benedict Arnold forcing his presence on a room. Peggy speaks in the plain thee and thou of her Quaker upbringing, as the front picture's caption shows. Readers get a girl's-eye view of the war's last year, mixing home duties, danger, and loyalty to country. The tale closes with chapters named Verified Suspicions and Lights Out.
36961-the-girl-from-his-town:
The Girl from His Town is a novel by Marie Van Vorst, published at Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1910. Pictures by Graham Cootes run through the book. The tale brings a young American west into the drawing rooms of London.

Dan Blair charms the Duchess of Breakwater at first sight. His slang is beyond her, but his quick look, bright smile, and new gayness win her. American men were not liked in that set, and Lady Galorey does not even announce him at the first shoot. The girl of the title is Letty Lane, a singer from Dan's own town. Chapters take the pair from a stage entrance to the Carlton and to Maxim's. A prince accepts at the end of the long list, and a soda-water fountain girl stands in the last chapters.
37414-the-world-turned-upside-down:
Clayton wrote this topsy-turvy tale book for children, and Dean and Son printed it in London. The World Turned Upside Down opens its fun with the foolish coat. Things speak, masters serve, and nothing sits in its place.

The coat is in a downright rage, whisking his tails like an angry lion. To be beaten, caned, cuffed, and shaken two or three times a day, he cries, is a shame. If you were not well thrashed, says the cane, you would soon grow thick with dust. So I say, remarks the hat. Nobody ever hits you, the coat fires back, and if they did, you could hit back. The hat at least has his own soft brush. Dutch plates colour the joke, in Dean's Christmas-book style.
39403-historic-fredericksburg-the-story-:
Goolrick's Historic Fredericksburg, the story of an old town, was printed at Richmond, Virginia, in 1922, with photographs by the Davis Gallery of Fredericksburg. One plate shows President Harding on the Wilderness battlefield.

Chapters run from the older days of cabins on the river bank through the town's glory after the Revolution to the Civil War. Fredericksburg was shelled by 181 guns, fought over at Marye's Heights, and caught again in the struggles at Chancellorsville, the Wilderness, and the Bloody Angle. Later chapters honour the town's early heroes, its unforgotten women, its old court records, gardens, churches, and schools, and its 250th birthday. Goolrick writes local history as a love letter to his town.
39482-mushroom-town:
Mushroom Town is a novel by Oliver Onions, copyrighted in 1914. Doran published it in New York for Hodder and Stoughton. Onions had written Gray Youth and Debit Account before it. His dedication confesses to liberties taken with Wales. The town of Llanyglo in the book is on no map, he warns. It is a composite of features from real places.

Six years of Welsh kindness stand behind the fiction, Onions says. Much of the book writes down things told him by his hosts. Three parts trace the town's rise in quick time. The Year Dot and Its Nonage open the first part. Railhead and the clerk of the works mark the building boom. A holiday camp and a giant's stride come in the third part. A mushroom town is one that springs up overnight.
40980-the-life-of-david-or-the-history-o:
A life of David, king of old Israel, was set in print once more. This form comes from the book of 1766, its title says. Carlile of Fleet Street put it out in London. It is sent to Samuel Chandler with warm thanks. Chandler's keen notes had once put the small book to a hard test.

The author grants his book gained much from that test. What stood it is now held firm with more weight, he says. David is named the man after God's own heart in the title. His reign, wars, songs, and sins fill the life in turn. Church readers of that age prized such brief lives. Old spell and grave tone mark the prose.
41444-the-dogs-of-boytown:
Walter Dyer, who wrote Pierrot, Dog of Belgium, told this tale of boys and their dogs for Holt of New York in 1918. Romulus and Remus, two pup brothers, stand in a plate at the front. Sam Bumpus and his Nan open the story.

Sam's shack comes next, then the pups take their Roman names. In Rome is a joke chapter: the pups' names send the tale there. The Willowdale kennels and anxious days build the dog world. Rags and other dogs fill a middle part. The training of Romulus leads to the Boytown dog show. Camp Britches, the passing of Rags, and the trials close a warm, true book of dogs.
41729-kisington-town:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote Kisington Town, a book for young readers from Houghton Mifflin. The motto of the book is a blessing on the peacemakers. Brown gives it to the best of readers, her father and mother, who taught her the love of books. An old song at the front praises a jolly good book, in doors or out. Some tales here first ran in St Nicholas magazine, by kind leave of its publishers.

Harold leads the cast, in a siege of Kisington and a tale of Red Rex. The Dragon of Hushby takes three parts to tell in full. A bargain, a wonder-garden, and the king's coat of arms follow in turn. A lion passant, a hermit gnome, a robber, and a king's pie add fun. Brown gives children a town of tales, where small deeds win the day.
43156-unawares-a-story-of-an-old-french-:
Frances Peard wrote Unawares, a story of an old French town, issued by Roberts Brothers in Boston in an edition dated eighteen seventy two. Chapter one opens at a fountain in the town, under a line from Longfellow on a quaint old town of toil and traffic. Veuve Angelin is the knowing widow at the centre of town talk. A sick or dead man is the hot news.

Women crowd round Angelin at the fountain with a volley of shrill questions. Was it a fit, has Monsieur Deshoulières gone to him, is he dead, what becomes of her, they cry. Angelin, small and thin with twinkling black eyes, savours her advantage. It is not given to all to know more than neighbours, she reflects, nor is the privilege to be lightly parted with. A tale of French town life, gossip, and quiet hearts follows.
43553-letters-to-an-unknown:
Letters to an Unknown gathers letters by Prosper Merimee in English dress. Bigelow Brown of New York issued the volume in the Saintsbury edition. George Saintsbury edited the works of Merimee for this set of volumes. A portrait study of Merimee opens the book before the letters start.

The sketch shows a tall, erect, pale man with a cold distant manner. His face stayed still on formal occasions, and his voice stayed calm. Even his wittiest tales came in the tone of a man ordering tea. Feeling was mastered, not absent, the writer insists of the French author. The letters then show Merimee writing freely to one unnamed friend.
44149-in-pawn:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote a comic tale of a boy and his father that Houghton Mifflin published in 1921. Lem Redding has a dimple that comes when he smiles. His quick ways come from his dead mother. He is little like his father Harvey.

Harvey Redding is the laziest man in or near Riverbank, and one of the heaviest. His belt has stood at its last hole for years while he grows round it. He dozes in his hickory rocker every half hour of the day. When his lit pipe falls into the bosom of his shirt and burns him, he swears at all the world and almost rises. Butler sets the pair in a page: a lively boy, and a mountain of a man at rest.
44895-no-cross-no-crown:
William Penn wrote this discourse on the holy cross of Christ. Harvey and Darton printed the new edition in London, 1842. Living and dying testimonies of famed persons stand added to it. A Luke verse bids a man take up his cross daily.

The preface calls man great business to glorify God, save his soul. Man minds nothing less than what he should most mind, Penn writes. Pride, avarice, and luxury eat the days meant for blessedness steps. Disobedience to the law of God in his heart brought this. A crown of righteousness verse from Timothy stands beside the Luke text on the title.
45379-prairie-dog-town:
Prairie-Dog Town is a children's animal fantasy by Laura Bancroft, published at Chicago in 1906. Reilly and Britton issued it as one of the Twinkle Tales. Maginel Wright Enright drew the illustrations. Six volumes make up the series, from a woodchuck tale to Twinkle's Enchantment. Twinkle, the heroine, is a farmer's little girl in Dakota. Her town, Edgeley, stands on the edge of civilization.

Seventeen wooden houses, a school, a church, and a store make the town. Twinkle walks to school from the farm, in calico slips and sunbonnets. Her chum Chubbins is the schoolteacher's son. A picnic opens the eight chapters. Then comes Prairie Dog Town itself, with Bowko its mayor. A magician, the Puff Pudgys, and Teenty and Weenty follow. The mayor gives a luncheon before the children return to the upper earth.
45732-some-persons-unknown:
Some Persons Unknown, by Hornung, is a set of tales issued in New York in 1898. Hornung had written A Bride From the Bush and other books before this one. The book is given to the memory of his mother.

The first tale, Kenyon's Innings, opens on a boy of eleven who loves danger. Kenyon walks the high garden wall, climbs over the glasshouses, and straddles a gable of the house. His sister Ethel, still with her hair down, has sole charge of him for the day. The other tales range wide: a widow at Piper's Point, the voice of Gunbar, and a magic cigar. A governess at Greenbush, a farewell performance, and the star of the Grasmere round out the set.
45742-up-and-down:
Up and Down, by E F Benson, was printed at New York by George H Doran in 1918. Benson also wrote Dodo and David Blaize. The book is a diary in months, from May 1914 to April 1917, with the war years in its bones. It opens in May 1914 with a hymn to Italy. Benson feels some Latin thread in his blood each time the train slips from the Alpine tunnels into the south.

Venice holds him first: still canals, dim churches, and the glow of Bellini and Tintoret. Florence at dawn, Rome at dusk, and Naples and Assisi each cast their own spell. Yet the spell, he says, is Italy itself, found best on bare hills where vines climb the trees. Travel fans get a lover's notes from the last spring of the old world.
46004-neighbors-unknown:
Charles Roberts wrote Neighbors Unknown, a book of wild animal tales, for Macmillan at New York in 1911. The tales had rights held from 1909 and 1910 by magazine houses. Roberts gives the book to Patricia. It opens on the roof of the world, a flat waste under Arctic night. Small hills, mere knobs and humps, stress the vast, shelterless flat around them. Somewhere below the levels, sea ends and land begins, yet snow hides the line.

More tales treat a black swamp, an isle of birds, and the antlers of the caribou. A sentry of the sedge-flats, a tree-top aeronaut, and a torpedo in feathers follow. One tale tells how a cat played Robinson Crusoe on her own. Gray lynx hunts for the last time, and mothers of the north close the book.
4794-dawn:
Mrs. Harriet A. Adams published Dawn at Boston and London in 1868, opening with a married couple sitting together in twilight, conversing. Three years have swept over their married life, bringing their hearts closer. That night, as stars appear one by one, a heavenly calm rests on their spirits.

Then the wife asks Hugh whether he thinks very few marriages are harmonious. Hugh answers from deep experience with human nature and close observation of life that their own marriage, and a few happy exceptions beside, are but feeble offsets to countless unhappy unions. People, he says, are only married fractionally, knowing so little of themselves that they cannot know each other, and the greatest strangers to each other may share a home. Readers get a Victorian novel of marriage, happiness, and the question of what truly joins two lives.
48230-the-soul-of-john-brown:
Stephen Graham, an English traveller, wrote this book on Black life in the American South. Macmillan printed The Soul of John Brown in New York in 1920. Graham walked the South and set down what he saw, heard, and thought on the road.

Thoughts on Slavery opens the book, then Graham goes In Virginia. Orators, actors, preachers, and singers fill one chapter. He marches through Georgia, tramps to the sea, and weighs the vote after the war. Alabama brings his sharpest theme: colour and colour bias. Exodus, New Orleans, the new Negro mind, and Black leadership follow. He ends up the Mississippi at Vicksburg, in a land where the freed slaves of 1863 had grown to twelve million souls.
50092-illustrated-edition-of-the-life-an:
The Illustrated Edition of the Life and Escape of William Wells Brown from American Slavery was written by Brown himself. It was printed at London by Gilpin in 1851 and sold for one shilling. The title page calls it the fourteenth thousand. Brown was a fugitive slave who had become a lecturing agent of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society.

The book opens with testimonials to the friends of freedom in Europe, dated at Boston in July 1849. Their reasons are set out in order. For years he has given his time and talents, at great personal hazard, to the cause of his enslaved countrymen. The life that follows is Brown's own story of slavery and escape, one of the best known of the slave narratives.
50388-my-lady-peggy-goes-to-town:
Frances Aymar Mathews wrote this society tale, and Harrison Fisher drew its plates. My Lady Peggy Goes to Town came out in 1901. Then Lady Peggy, laughing — the first plate's line catches her key note whole.

Fisher was the age's great drawer of fine women, and his Peggy fits his fame: bright, poised, and lit for the town. A lady comes to town: calls, balls, and the game of hearts follow in due form. Mathews wrote knowing tales of rich American life, with its codes and its traps. The full-page plates are set by lines from the text, so picture and tale chase each other down the book.
5127-shakespeare-bacon-and-the-great-unk:
Andrew Lang's 1912 study takes up the old dispute over who wrote Shakespeare's plays. Lang answers the Baconians, who credited Francis Bacon, and other doubters, arguing from contemporary records, the First Folio. Men like Ben Jonson testify that William Shakespeare of Stratford was indeed the author.

Chapters weigh the rival claims, the history of the plays in print, and what Shakespeare's contemporaries actually said about him. Lang writes with wit and impatience toward conspiracy theories, and the book remains a readable defence of the traditional attribution, grounded in the documents of Shakespeare's own time.
51662-breakdown:
Herbert D Kastle wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Galaxy Magazine in June 1961, drawn by Cowles. A tag line asks how you keep them down on the farm after they have seen the truth. A farmer has suffered mixed up memories and thoughts for weeks. His wife Edna begs him to see the doctor two miles past Dugan's farm.

He refuses point blank to admit he is sick in the head. He concedes a man can grow forgetful, but no more. Lying in bed beside his wife, he feels the trouble pressing again. Kastle builds the tale on a rural mind coming apart, with a hint that the cause is no common illness.
53566-the-fate-of-a-crown:
The Fate of a Crown, a novel by Schuyler Staunton, was printed in Chicago in 1905. Its front plate names Lesba as daughter of the revolution. Chapter heads promise plots, a secret vault, and a death sentence. Names in the heads include General Fonseca and Dom Pedro de Alcantara. The tale mixes love, spies, and rebellion.

The story opens with the narrator watching his Uncle Nelson open the mail. One large blue envelope draws the old man's eye at once. He reads it twice and sets it apart from the rest. That small act signals a secret of weight. From there the plot moves through Valcour, Madam Izabel, and a man with a missing finger.
54331-life-of-a-pioneer-being-the-autobi:
James Brown tells his own life as a pioneer in western America. Cannon and Sons printed the autobiography at Salt Lake City in 1900. The preface says pioneer life is full of peril and hardship. Startling episodes and thrilling adventures mark such lives, it adds.

Brown was a frontiersman and Indian interpreter of notable experience there. He marched with the famous Mormon Battalion in its long service. He stood present at the finding of gold in California too. Pacific slope and Rocky Mountain gains frame his historic years of travel. Cannon and Sons printed the life at Salt Lake City.
55080-the-worst-boy-in-town:
The Worst Boy in Town is a tale by John Habberton, printed at New York in the late eighteen hundreds. The title page lists his past books for young and old readers. A note at the front points to a print form of the book with its first pictures, and to page scans held in a large archive.

The book is made out, with dry wit, to very bad boys, and to the fine old fellows who once bore that name. A first plate shows a sea jaunt gone wrong in a small boat. The shape is plain from the start: a comic tale of a boys pranks and scrapes, told for laughs, with a soft close look at how a town names a boy bad.
56242-the-gates-of-dawn:
The Gates of Dawn, a novel by Fergus Hume, was published in London in 1894 by Sampson Low, Marston. A motto verse promises that grief flies at midnight and joy comes up through the gates of dawn. Thirty chapters mix village gossip, palmistry, letters to a London friend, a recluse, and a gipsy's prophecy. Farbis Court and its portrait gallery anchor the scene.

Chapter one, The Pleasures of the Road, opens on a caravan rolling slowly down a dusty road. The van is painted dark green, with white-curtained windows picked out in rose pink and bright red shafts and wheels. Hume, famed for a hansom cab mystery, here turns to a rural tale of travel, old houses, and slow romance.
56469-five-years-in-a-persian-town:
Five Years in a Persian Town is a travel and residence account by Napier Malcolm, published in New York by Dutton in 1905. The town is Yezd. A frontispiece plate of Yezdi types, numbered and captioned, opens the volume.

The plate shows a tunnel digger who brings water from the hills, a Parsi farmer, a porter, a muleteer, an oil seller with his gourds, and a dervish. The first chapter treats the district, its desert, water supply, gardens, and houses built for heat. Later chapters take up isolation, the town as a political unit, and Persian Mohammedanism. Malcolm writes from five years of living where few Europeans stayed. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
56753-satanella-a-story-of-punchestown:
Satanella, a story of Punchestown, is a novel by Whyte Melville, the famed writer of hunting and racing tales. Lucy Kemp Welch drew the illustrations. The first chapter is called The Black Mare, and the front picture shows a rider brought on his head by a fall. Miss Douglas and Daisy enter early, and Mrs Lushington follows.

Chapters proceed through cutting for partners, getting on, and a spell at sea. Cormac's Town and Punchestown itself bring the tale to the races. Winners and losers, a garden of Eden, Soldier Bill, and Delilah fill the middle. A debt of honour and a snake in the grass darken the later pages. Whyte Melville knew the Irish racing world at first hand. His tale mixes horse dealing, love, and the gamble of the turf, in the sporting style that made his name with country readers.
5686-four-months-in-a-sneak-box-a-boat-v:
Nathaniel H. Bishop recounts a long small-boat voyage down American rivers toward the Gulf of Mexico, made in a sneak-box built for shallow water and frequent carries over land. The opening chapters describe the boat itself, its builder, and its haul to the Ohio River, then trace the sources of the Ohio through the Monongahela and Allegheny rivers. Maps drawn for the work by the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey mark the Gulf coast in unusual detail.

The book blends travel narrative with practical boating knowledge, noting currents, portages, towns, and the people met along the way. Readers who enjoy river journeys will find a steady, observant account of life afloat, where progress is measured in miles, weather, and safe landings. It also preserves a picture of nineteenth-century river country before rail and road changed its pace.
5697-tales-of-chinatown:
Sax Rohmer's Tales of Chinatown, published in 1916, gathers stories of London's Limehouse underworld, where detectives, adventurers, and shadowy figures cross paths. Its contents include The Daughter of Huang Chow, Kerry's Kid, The Pigtail of Hi Wing Ho, The House of Golden Joss, and The Hand of the Mandarin, among others. The opening tale begins in a public-house saloon bar with a figure called Diamond Fred.

Rohmer writes for sensation: secret societies, hidden rooms, sudden violence, and exotic detail drive each tale. Modern readers should note that the stories carry the period's stereotypes of Chinese people, which are part of their dated flavor and a reason to read them critically. As popular fiction, the book shows how early twentieth-century thrillers built suspense from fog, rumor, and the lure of a forbidden quarter.
57844-the-adventures-of-jimmy-brown:
The Adventures of Jimmy Brown is a humorous boys' book written by Jimmy himself and edited by Alden. Harper published it in New York; the copyright is 1885. A picture shows the unexpected results of Jimmy's efforts to trap pigs. The contents list short scrapes in order: a game, a scalp, a private circus, burglars.

Jimmy's neighbour Martin suffers through many chapters, losing an eye, a leg, and his temper by turns. A monkey comes and ends. Ice cream, a bull-fight, a balloon, and a steam chair fill the later pages. Alden writes the mischief in a boy's own deadpan voice. The book was a favourite of American boy humour in its day.
58282-to-london-town:
Arthur Morrison tells an East End tale in To London Town, printed at Leipzig in 1899 in the Tauchnitz edition. Morrison had writ Tales of Mean Streets and A Child of the Jago. He gives the book to Lady Dorothy Nevill.

A note sets the book among its mates. He designed and began it between the two earlier books, he says, and it should be read together with those. No one of the three paints a complete picture of life in the eastern parts of London, he grants. Each fills out the other two. The tale opens on a bright afternoon by Epping Thicks. The August air freshens, and greenwoods heave in the wind. An old man and a crippled child take an errant path down to Wormleyton Pits.
5845-the-story-of-a-calico-clown:
The Story of a Calico Clown opens on a toy counter in a big department store, where toys talk after hours. An elephant from Noah's Ark speaks to a double-humped camel in the next stall. Tonight, he says, they shall have a most wonderful time. Nearby, a Jack in the Box sways to and fro on his spring. The giant's swing promises a night of toy adventure.

Young readers find a calico clown and his toy companions in a world where playthings wake when shops close. The story favors gentle wonder over fright, with each toy's character shaping its fun. It suits early readers and read-aloud families who enjoy toy tales, and it pairs naturally with other stories of dolls and animals coming alive at night.
5874-dawn:
Dawn opens with a boy's fourteenth birthday and a discovery he will soon call the Great Terror. Keith Burton receives Treasure Island from his father as a birthday present. To his surprise and distress, it is printed in type so blurred and poor that he can scarcely read it. He does not know the terror by that name until some days afterward, when its meaning grows clearer.

Here follows a young hero facing a shadow over his reading, his play, and his future, in a story that favors feeling over explanation. The novel's power lies in its opening image: a beloved book made unreadable. It suits readers who enjoy coming-of-age tales with a mystery at their heart, and those who like stories where a small, strange fact changes a life.
58964-roadtown:
Roadtown, by Edgar Chambless, sets out a plan to remake social life. The Roadtown Press issued it at New York with rights in 1910. Chambless dedicates it, with bite, to Morgan, a straight player of a crooked game. Losses on railroad stocks set him thinking, he tells the reader at once.

John Haynes Holmes introduces the man and his dream of Roadtown living. Holmes met him as one more visionary with a scheme two years before. The plan grew from crude notion to tested design in that time. Roadtown promises a straight game where any may play fair and win. Linear town life along a road is the heart of the scheme.
58974-our-town:
Jerome Bixby wrote a bleak tale first printed in Worlds of If in February 1955. Enemy jets strike Smoky Creek, Tennessee, a town of 123 souls. Small atom bombs wreck the bridge, tracks, and road, and kill all in town. Just twenty-one old folk live, since they were at a picnic in the woods.

Three months on, an enemy jet comes back to sniff the dead valley. The old folk, left with grief and memory, face a foe they cannot fight as the young once could. Bixby asks what pride and loss do when a whole town ends at a stroke. The short tale hits hard and stays stark.
60737-to-each-his-own:
Jack Sharkey wrote a science fiction tale that ran in Worlds of If in January 1960. Its head note warns that a world ideal for life will have life on it, but don't expect ideal life. On September the 24th, 1965, the Venusian spaceship Investigator floated gently to Earth in Times Square. The sleek metal belly touched feather light on the asphalt X of Broadway and Seventh Avenue.

Stubby stabilizing legs extended, bracing the ship against rolling. It hulks like a metallic beetle at rest. The sun stands almost directly overhead, sending gold glints across the hull. Sharkey sets first contact at America's most photographed crossroads. The title promises each species its own portion.
61374-countdown:
Countdown is a science tale by Grow, first set in a pulp sheet in the early nineteen sixties. Its first lines count down with care: the moment is at hand, the fingers are poised, this is what comes next. A note tells that no proof was found its rights were made new in law.

Ten years of ill peace have passed since the Hour of Tragedy, the text says. Ten tense years rank with fear, hate, and doubt. Ten units out of the vast count of time, the dim, fixed, void span. Nine worlds spin, nine spawn of the sun. One of them is new born, a hair from its birth right. But which birth right? It can choose: the warm growth of its parent star, or the stars pure fire.
61387-rundown:
Robert Lory wrote this tale of a panhandler with a special purpose. The story ran in Worlds of If in May 1963. A subway train screeches into Westboro station as it opens. A man is shoved from the car by the eight o clock crowd.

He was not asleep, yet he cannot say he was aware either. The station name means nothing to him as he stares. He is lost and cannot recall what he is lost from. Crowds jostle him to the cold cement floor in the rush. A dirty man in a torn white shirt is what he sees when he looks down.
62799-john-brown:
John Brown is a life in the American Crisis Biographies series of lives. Ellis Paxson Oberholtzer edited the series for readers of the sectional struggle. Each volume is a cloth duodecimo with a front portrait, priced one dollar twenty five. Southern writers took Southern subjects and Northern writers Northern ones by design.

The series aims to tell the whole sectional struggle through single lives. Its list runs from Abraham Lincoln and Thomas Benton to Farragut and Sherman. Frederick Douglass by Booker Washington and Robert Lee stand in the list. Judah Benjamin, Jefferson Davis, and Alexander Stephens fill out the Southern side. Brown life gives the abolitionist captain place in that impartial plan.
63076-the-yarn-of-old-harbour-town:
The Yarn of Old Harbour Town is a sea novel by Clark Russell. Fisher Unwin published it in London in 1905. This copy is the second impression of the novel. Russell also wrote The Romance of a Midshipman. An old rhyme from 1835 fronts the title page as an epigraph. Its ballad tells of a ship sweeter than any lady. The captain made sail with the lady when the hatches were flush. The contents list chapters named for the chief people.

Lucy Acton and Walter Lawrence open the story in turn. The Offer and a ship called the Aurora follow. Two chapters ask where the Minorca and where Lucy have gone. A visit from a lawyerly Mr Greyquill comes later in the list. Princess Tatters stands out among the chapter titles. The yarn mixes a port town romance with a missing ship mystery.
63458-pussy-cat-town:
Pussy Cat Town is a book for children by Marion Ames Taggart, dated 1906 in the record. It belongs to the Roses of Saint Elizabeth series of gift books. Each book in that series was a small quarto with colour pictures. The price of each was one dollar to the buyer.

A town of cats gives the tale its name and its charm. Children of that age loved animal towns with streets and shops of their own. Taggart wrote many books for young readers and for girls. Her touch here is playful, with pictures to carry the fancy. The series dress made the book a gift for Christmas and birthdays. Colour plates and fine binding set it apart from cheap story papers.
63731-syria-the-desert-the-sown:
Syria, the Desert and the Sown is a travel book by Gertrude Lowthian Bell. Dutton of New York brought the book out in the year 1907. John Sargent's Bedouins of the Syrian Desert fronts the volume here. Many illustrations and a map back the tale of her journeys. Fourteen chapters and an index close the book of the East.

Jerusalem fills the early plates: the Mosque of Umar, the Holy Sepulchre. Russian pilgrims and baptism in Jordan stand among the pictured scenes. The monastery of Mar Saba and the Wall of Lamentation follow on. The theatre at Amman, ruined churches, and Roman milestones crowd the road. Mshitta's facade and inner halls win plates of their own here. Desert wells, watering camels, and striking camp close the picture list. Bell knew the heart of the East, her dedication hints warmly.
63892-fourth-down:
Ralph Henry Barbour wrote this school football novel, published by Appleton in 1920. Arnold Deering and Frank Lamson ride the train back to Yardley, grousing about the hard year ahead and the way vacations spoil a boy for work.

The contents chart a season: new quarters, Sid's advice, Tubb trying football, and Yardley playing Greenburg. Later chapters put Toby at quarter, bring a tough bunch, an accident, and a quarter-back run. The last chapter is the title itself, Fourth Down. Barbour wrote a long shelf of school sport stories, and this one runs his classic pattern: the second team, promotion earned, and the big game decided at the end.
64665-an-exciting-new-year-s-day-in-jung:
Beulah Mary Crocker tells a winter animal tale in An Exciting New Year's Day in Jungletown, printed by the Press of Hahn and Harmon Company of Minneapolis and copyrighted in 1910. The first of January dawns bright and clear, to the joy of all Jungletown, for King Leo has decreed sporting contests on Monkey Hill.

Foot races on skis and snowshoes, snowball fights, and toboggan races fill the day, though the king bans skating from his games. The squirrels beat the bears at skiing, being lighter on their feet, and the giraffes win the snowshoe race. A toboggan load of monkeys brings the danger.
64940-the-fantasy-fan-volume-2-number-2-:
The Fantasy Fan is a monthly magazine made by and for science fiction fans. Hornig edited it from Elizabeth, New Jersey. He also managed a professional story magazine. An issue cost ten cents. This number is the second of volume two, from 1934. Its whole number is fourteen.

A letter column called Our Readers Say fills the opening pages. The editor announces a new custom. Each issue will honour a person or a theme. Lovecraft receives the first dedication. Long instalments of his essay on supernatural horror run in the magazine. This instalment deals wholly with Poe. Readers praise poems and tales from the August issue. Lovecraft himself writes in praise of the sketches.
64942-the-fantasy-fan-volume-2-number-5-:
The Fantasy Fan, the fans own magazine, volume two, number five, whole number seventeen, for January nineteen thirty five, cost ten cents a copy or a dollar a year. Charles D Hornig edited the monthly from Elizabeth, New Jersey; he also managed Wonder Stories. The number is a special weird poetry number. A Forward by the editor opens it. The next issue will be a special short story number, he promises.

The March issue will be dedicated to Weird Tales, Hornig adds. F Lee Baldwin has compiled an excellent biography of H P Lovecraft for it, with a wood cut by Duane W Rimel, he notes. Material is coming from Seabury Quinn, Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and Robert E Howard, he says. The Our Readers Say department is dropped with this issue. Fan historians get a prime fanzine of the Lovecraft circle.
65377-flight-into-the-unknown:
Flight Into the Unknown, by Tom Harris, ran in Imagination in August 1957. The tale follows young Bailey on his first trip into space. A meteor hulled the ship, he thinks, and flung the crew out like seeds from a burst pod.

Bailey falls alone through the dark, screaming as icy space rushes at his face. Then light breaks in, and Captain DiCredico is shaking him awake aboard the Ranger. He is safe, yet his body still swears that he is falling. The captain orders the ship spun, and a light false gravity settles his nerves. The hull becomes down, and men walk once more. Dread, though, has a hold on Bailey that spin alone cannot cure.
67361-bob-bowen-comes-to-town:
Bob Bowen Comes to Town, a story by Bedford Jones, opens in the smoking room of a train crossing central California. A fat man complains of the heat; a drummer from San Francisco argues mining stock with a lean man, doubting ruby silver. It has too much arsenic, he has heard, and comes in small veins.

Sometimes, the lean man answers, smiling. Tonopah was founded on ruby silver, and the Yellow Jack, the richest mine there, busted into it. Mining sharks wired east, and their principals paid a million and a half for the property. The drummer demands how he knows. I am the man who sold out the Yellow Jack, says the lean man, handing over his card: Bob Bowen, on his way to Frisco to sell a couple more mines. The fat man leans forward: his name is Dickover, of New York, who knows Bowen.
67366-the-cap-and-gown:
The Cap and Gown, by Charles Reynolds Brown, is a book of talks to college men, copyrighted in 1910 and printed by the Pilgrim Press. Brown also wrote The Social Message of the Modern Pulpit and Faith and Health. His first chapter, The First Inning, warns that the first year in college can scarcely be overrated in its weight.

Later chapters treat athletics, the fraternity question, and the religion of a college man. The choice of a life work, moral ventures, and the law of returns follow, with a closing chapter on the war against war. Brown likens the freshman to the first man at bat, watched by all, his early hits setting the keynote.
67883-the-end-of-elfintown:
The End of Elfintown is a verse tale by Jane Barlow with cuts by Laurence Housman. A Macmillan house of London brought the book out in eighteen ninety four. King Oberon of the elves falls under a bad brown witch spell in the verse. She shows him in her mere glass a grand town of days to come. Its towers, marts, streets, jails, and halls all stand shrunk to elf eye range.

That town dream haunts his heart when the witch wipes the glass clean. No beam, breeze, or shade gives him joy from that day on. Glow worm lamps burn dim and king cup gold looks dull to his eyes. Bed shifts from hare bell tent to fox glove hall bring no rest. His court stands round and moans the change in whispers at dusk.
68783-the-swamp-was-upside-down:
The Swamp Was Upside Down is a science fiction story by Murray Leinster. It appeared in the magazine Astounding Science Fiction in September 1956. Freas drew the pictures for it. The tale opens aboard a Survey ship falling toward its destination.

Hardwick, a senior officer of the Colonial Survey, feels the ship turn end for end. Artificial gravity holds his feet to the floor, but his ears report the tumble. The manoeuvre kills the drive's momentum as the ship nears its goal. Then a young officer brings him changed orders in the wardroom. The ship will not land after all, he is told. Hardwick must go down to the surface by boat instead. The ship had spent months on no other errand than fetching him.
69474-a-modern-trio-in-an-old-town:
A Modern Trio in an Old Town, by Katharine Haviland Taylor, was published in nineteen twenty-two by Harcourt, Brace and Company of New York. Morgan Dennis illustrated the novel. Taylor had already written Real Stuff, Natalie Page, and Barbara of Baltimore.

The narrator looks back on her eighteen years and confesses her apprehensions were usually foolish. Parties she dreaded proved lively, while promising ones left her smiling until her face ached. The old town of the title is Florence, Italy. Chapters cover a Florentine winter, Fiesole on a clear hot day, and a country wedding in spring. Sam Deane enters at chapter eleven, and Cupid works mischievously before the homeward bound close. The trio of the title are young Americans learning Italy and each other.
70175-the-secret-of-father-brown:
The Secret of Father Brown is a set of crime tales by Chesterton, of his famed small priest who solves crimes by their soul. It was first set in print in the late nineteen twenties, at London and in towns of the Crown round the world. Its gift word makes it out to a real priest of Bradford.

That priests truth, it says, is more strange than tale craft, with a thanks more great than the world. Its parts name their crimes in plain style: a judge and his glass, a man with two beards, a song of a fly fish, an actor and his plea. A lost lord, the worst crime in the world, and a red moon fill the rest.
72093-a-study-of-mushrooms-and-mushroom-:
A Study of Mushrooms and Mushroom Spawn, by Edward H Jacob of West Chester, Pennsylvania, was copyrighted in nineteen fourteen by the author. Jacob wrote as a grower with large and successful experience of mushroom culture for the markets. His preface admits he met failure after failure at first.

Poor spawn and bad beds caused most of those failures, he says. That history, he argues, qualifies him to guide beginners better than a theorist could. He promises concise, accurate information without misleading or extravagant statements. The opening section is called the source of success. The pamphlet addresses home and local growers rather than great commercial houses. American mushroom growing was then a young trade, and spawn quality decided fortunes.
72861-head-hunters-black-white-and-brown:
Head Hunters, Black, White, and Brown, by Alfred C Haddon, was printed in London by Methuen in 1901. Haddon lectured on ethnology at Cambridge. Thirty two plates, forty text figures, and six maps fill the book. He gives it to his wife and to the memory of his mother.

Haddon records his travels with a science party to the islands north of Australia and to New Guinea. A welcome letter from the government at Thursday Island stands near the start. The Hon John Douglas gave the party every help in his power, in office and in private. The title plays on head hunting among island peoples, set by the side of white and brown ways. Students of peoples get a rich field record from a founder of the craft.
73312-the-daughter-of-the-dawn:
The Daughter of the Dawn, a tale of Maori magic by William Reginald Hodder, came from L C Page at Boston in 1903, with art by Harold Piffard. The book is given to an old pair at the foot of Taranaki, their lives as pure as its snow. Plate notes whet the taste: a long form hangs over a dark gulf. A stone head's brows rise from black. A flash shows Crystal in her night dress on a path.

The first words set the frame. Hodder sits late in his Harley Street room as the cabs thin out, and an odd sense of wait creeps in. The record of Wanaki has come to his hands by a strange road, and his task is to shape it. Tale fans get spell, stone, and dawn in the isles.
74174-mr-biggs-goes-to-town:
Mr Biggs Goes to Town, a story by Nelson Bond, ran in Amazing Stories in October 1942. Lancelot Biggs makes soap on an asteroid in this series of comic tales. When he started that business there, he got strange results, the blurb warns. The narrator waits in a cradle on Earth for flight orders.

Two owl eyed men in white mess jackets march into the control turret. They carry frowns and a slip of paper with the crew names. Herbert Donovan answers present, with a joke on the side.
