Bond wrote the Biggs tales as space farce with a tall tale swing. A soap maker in the sky lanes is his kind of hero. The humour runs on bluster, luck, and cosmic red tape.
7463-darkness-and-dawn:
George Allan England's trilogy, dedicated to Robert H. Davis, opens with a world gone dark. Its first book is called The Vacant World. Its chapters run from The Awakening and The City of Death to A Thousand Years, The Gathering of the Hordes, and Eve Becomes an Amazon. The story wakes its people in a ruined city, long after civilization has fallen.

Exploration, treasure, terror, and war follow as the survivors learn what the new world holds: strange races, an unknown menace, and the question of how humanity might begin again. England wrote the trilogy for readers of adventure romance, and it became a classic of early science fiction. The volume collects a tale of collapse and rebirth, told at a gallop.
76983-skeeter-bill-comes-to-town:
Skeeter Bill Comes to Town is a novelet by W C Tuttle. Tuttle tells of William Harrison Sarg, called Skeeter Bill, a salty seven footer bound for Yellow Butte for a kid birthday. On the way he does some fast shooting.

Skeeter leans at the bar of the only saloon in Temple Rock and studies the fly specked back bar. He stands at least seven feet tall in high heels and sombrero, with wide shoulders, a wasp waist, and long skinny legs. A homemade gun belt holds a Colt low on his thigh. His face is long and thin, with high cheek bones and green tinted eyes. He is not handsome, yet he looks efficient. His one bar vice is pop, and only if ice cold. Western fans get Tuttle humor and gun craft.
77038-trading-in-scrabbletown:
Trading in Scrabbletown is a local history by Alice Brayton, drawn from a barrel of old papers. The preface tells how the material was found for the book by its maker. John Summerfield Brayton gave a barrel of papers to the Fall River Historical Society in the summer of 1948. There were over four thousand papers in the barrel, well preserved, though some had been nibbled by mice.

 The papers concern trading in Scrabbletown, an old suburb of Swansea in Massachusetts, near Fall River. Trading a dull subject? By no means, the preface answers its own question in the text. The traders of Scrabbletown led a most exciting life by that account, packed with adventure and steadied by responsibility. Brayton book is micro history before the name existed, rebuilt from store papers and letters.
77258-life-of-john-brown:
Life of John Brown is a short biography pamphlet by Michael Gold, issued in 1924 as a Little Blue Book. The cheap pocket format was meant for working readers, and the tone matches it. A foreword sets John Brown beside Jesus and Socrates as a man proved by devotion to a cause.

The telling starts from slavery's respectability, the background chapter arguing that Brown can only be understood through the America that made slavery normal. Gold stresses that Brown was a plain, poor farmer with a large family, hanged as an outlaw. Only after the Civil War fulfilled his warnings was he seen as a great figure. The pamphlet closes its foreword by claiming Brown's soul still marches in the obscure heroes who fight for freedom in America today.
77768-marshal-of-sundown:
Jackson Gregory wrote a western tale of the marshal of a wild town. Grosset and Dunlap issued Marshal of Sundown in New York by pact with Dodd, Mead. Rights rest from 1937 and 1938 with the author. The tale opens on a live-oak knoll above the town of Sundown.

Jim Torrance rides in from the south with a boy, Skeeter, and a string of horses. Sundown looks clean and peaceful from three miles off at midday. Jim warns that the calm holds only till first-drink time in town. Western fans get a fast tale of grit, guns, and a town to tame.
78309-memoir-of-catharine-brown:
Rufus Anderson wrote Memoir of Catharine Brown in 1825. Samuel T Armstrong and partners issued it at Boston. Brown was a Christian Indian of the Cherokee Nation. Anderson served the American Board of Foreign Missions. He was its assistant secretary at the time. A front plate shows Brown on her sick bed.

She raised herself there to tell God's work on her soul. A tear fell as she spoke with a sweet smile. That scene stands at page 142 of the book. The copyright entry dates to December 1824. Armstrong claimed the book's rights in that filing. Mission memoirs like this raised funds and faith at once. A Cherokee convert's deathbed faith stands here as a model held up to church readers across the young republic.
78485-the-george-and-the-crown:
The George and the Crown, by Sheila Kaye-Smith, first appeared in 1925. Cassell published the novel in London and New York. Kaye-Smith had written Joanna Godden and Sussex Gorse before. She gives the book to Stern, a fellow writer. A prologue stands before three parts. The parts are named the Valley, the Island, and the Sea. Thomas Sheather, the prologue says, was born in the Ouse valley of Sussex. His home lay between Lewes and Newhaven. Kitty le Couteur lived at the Peche a Agneau, on Sark. They met and married all the same, in the island church of Peter the Fisherman. Its walls hold memorials of the drowned.

Tom reached Guernsey on a Deal coaster in the tomato season. Repairs kept him ashore for weeks, and he met Kitty in St Peter Port.
78534-keeping-the-lawn:
Keeping the Lawn, by Leonard Barron, was published at Newburgh, New York, in 1921. Barron edited The Garden Magazine when he wrote the guide. The Coldwell Lawn Mower Company issued the book as its own publication. The lawn is the dominant feature of the American home garden, it opens.

You may have green grass and nothing else and get a fair setting for a house, he writes. But never a satisfying home comes from the house without the lawn, he holds. The lawn is the essential base of country, suburban, and rural homes in his view. It sets country apart from city with its paved yards, he observes in the text. Grass as the canvas of the home grounds painter fills this maker handbook.
7950-the-jealousies-of-a-country-town:
Honoré de Balzac's two linked tales about the town of Alençon are gathered here under their shared French heading, Les Rivalités. The first, An Old Maid, comes in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, and the second, The Collection of Antiquities, in Ellen Marriage's; George Saintsbury supplies the introduction. Both stories turn on the Chevalier de Valois and the fading old nobility of a provincial town.

Balzac studies how birth, money, marriage, and reputation decide a small community's fortunes, with rivalries that run through both tales. Read together, the pair shows his method at full strength: a whole social world built from manners, households, and old grudges. It is a good entry point for readers new to his great cycle of French life, and a satisfying one for those already following it.
79630-in-the-town:
In the Town is a book of London verses by Douglas Goldring, published in London by Selwyn and Blount in 1916. Twenty of the verses were printed for the first time in the book. A few had appeared in magazines, and the rest came from an earlier volume called Streets. Goldring had written travel books on the Loire and on dream cities.

His opening poem calls London the great grey city that bred him and his. Supreme, mysterious, dirty and divine, it is made up of contrast, light and gloom. It has green hills and parks where flowers bloom, and shadowed pathways for lovers. It has deserts of humble brick and crowded centres of light and cheer. Thronged streets jostle theatre and hotel, while stately terraces house the rich. Black alleys, foul slums and palaces, prisons and spires fill the count. A Londoner's book of streets, written in wartime.
79681-the-hour-before-the-dawn:
The Hour Before the Dawn is an appeal to men from the Social Purity Alliance. Trübner and Company issued the book in London in eighteen hundred seventy six. The group was formed to press two root claims on the land. The home is sacred, and men owe pure lives to all.

No pledge binds a member who joins the Alliance ranks. Each must sway his own circle to a finer tone of life. Those who have strayed must be won back with kind aid. Women caught in vice should gain honest work and a fresh start. Talks, meetings, and hands on help form the group’s tools. Forms wait at Eight Bedford Row for those who would join. A Latin line from Paul fronts it: night is far spent. Watchman, what of the night, the appeal asks of its men.
79743-kings-and-queens-i-have-known:
Kings and Queens I Have Known, by Helene Vacaresco, was published in nineteen oh four by Harper and Brothers in London and New York. Twelve illustrations accompany the portraits in words. Vacaresco was a Roumanian poet who moved in courts and salons. She dedicates the book to the sovereigns themselves, in gratitude for personal kindness.

The contents begin with Queen Elizabeth of Roumania, the poet-queen Carmen Sylva. Edward the Seventh and Queen Alexandra follow, then the Emperor of Austria and the German Emperor. The Czar and Czarina, the Italian and Spanish courts, and Queen Wilhelmina appear in turn. The sovereigns of Servia, Pope Leo the Thirteenth, and Queen Victoria close the gallery. Written before nineteen fourteen, the book preserves the vanished ease of Europe's crowned cousins.
8219-the-desert-and-the-sown:
Mary Hallock Foote wrote The Desert and the Sown, a novel of the American West whose chapters run from a council of elders and introducing a son-in-law. Through an initial love, a man with a well in his own court. Disinherited, an appeal to nature, and a hunter's diary, to the power of weakness, the white peril. A searching of hearts, the blood-wite, a bridegroom of snow, the nature of an oath, and pilgrims and strangers. Later chapters reach a station in the desert, Indian summer, the fell frost, and peace.

Foote, who lived the western life she described, writes about irrigation, land, and marriage with the authority of experience. Her desert is both landscape and moral testing ground. For readers of western fiction, the novel offers a woman's perspective on settlement, richer in character than in gunplay, and beautifully observed.
9149-the-gray-dawn:
Stewart Edward White wrote this novel of old San Francisco, called here The Grey Dawn. Its chief figures are Milton Keith, a young lawyer from Baltimore, and his wife Nan. They land in a raw, gold-rich city where law is thin and men scheme for land, votes, and power. Mrs. Morrell plots revenge in the opening pages.

White, known for western tales, paints the city with a journalist's eye for detail and a novelist's pace. Gambling halls, claims, and court fights crowd the plot. The book remains a vivid portrait of California in the years when a frontier town grew into a great city.
9397-the-green-satin-gown:
Laura Richards wrote these stories in 1903 for the girls of the Friday Club of Gardiner, Maine, to whom the book is dedicated. The title tale asks who ever wore such a queer-looking thing, and answers: I wore it myself, dear, once upon a time. Other tales include Blue Egyptians, Little Benjamin, and Don Alonzo.

The Shed Chamber, Maine to the Rescue, and The Scarlet Leaves complete the set, with pictures by Etheldred Barry. Richards, known for Captain January, writes with humor and heart. The book remains a charming girls' story collection, warm, funny, and old-fashioned in the best sense.
britannica-1911-acerra-town:
Acerra is a town and episcopal see in Campania, Italy, in the province of Caserta, nine miles north-east of Naples, with more than sixteen thousand people in 1901. It lies on the right bank of the Agno in a fertile but marshy district that was badly malarial in the middle ages. Two other ancient towns shared the name Acerrae, in Umbria and in northern Italy.

Roman history fills the entry. Acerra gained Latin rights in 332 B.C. and became a municipium, a self-governing town. Hannibal destroyed it in 216 B.C., Rome restored it, and in the Social War it served as Roman headquarters and held out against the insurgents. Augustus planted a colony there, though river floods hurt the town.
britannica-1911-acre-town:
Acre, or Akka, is a port town of Palestine. It stands on a low promontory at the bay's north end. Tyre lies twenty-five miles north of it. About eleven thousand people lived there. Most were Moslems, with Christians and Jews besides. People long called Acre the Key of Palestine. Its shore commands the plain toward Esdraelon. That plain gives the easiest entry to the interior.

History here is chequered and calamitous. Egyptian lists name the town about 1500 B.C. The Old Testament mentions it once, as Acco. Crusaders made it their chief Palestinian port. Saladin retook it, then Richard recaptured it in 1191. The Franks lost it for good in 1291. Trade now drifts to Haifa, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-archangel-town:
Archangel is the chief town of Archangel government, Russia. It stands at the Dvina delta's head. Its latitude is 64 degrees 32 minutes north. Population in 1897 was 20,933. Norsemen frequented Bjarmeland on trading expeditions early. Ottar's voyage of about 880 is famous. Alfred the Great described that voyage. The modern town dates from 1553, though.

Richard Chancellor's visit founded its fortunes then. An English factory rose on the lower Dvina. A fort followed in 1584. The town grew around that fort. Archangel was long Russia's only seaport. Boris Godunov opened its trade to all nations. England, Holland, and Germany traded chiefly there. Peter the Great founded St Petersburg in 1702. He then hampered Archangel's commerce deliberately. Its trade declined under those disabilities. Daylight extremes mark its northern position.
britannica-1911-ashburton-town:
Ashburton is a market town in Devonshire, England. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its site, church, trades, and past. It lies in a hill-ringed valley near the river Dart. A rail branch served the town, and its 1901 count was about twenty-six hundred.

The church of Saint Andrew was built early in the 1400s. It holds a fine oak roof and a tablet to a famed lord from the town. A grammar school there dates to a chantry founded in 1314. Serge cloth making, brewing, paint works, and sawmills gave work. Nearby Buckfast Abbey was restored for French monks in 1882. The town was an old stannary borough that once sent members to Parliament.
britannica-1911-baku-town:
Baku is the chief town of its Russian government. It stands on the Apsheron peninsula's south side. Railways link it to the Black Sea ports. Batum lies 560 miles away by rail. A long stone quay backs the harbour. The new town climbs slopes behind it.

The old town lies westward there. Steep, narrow, winding streets fill it. Its look is decidedly oriental. A native khans' palace survives in ruins. Persian shahs built mosques in 1078. The maidens' tower now serves as lighthouse. Russian Caspian fleet works line the harbour. Petroleum refineries lead the town's industry. Flour mills and tobacco factories follow. Baku depots Persian and Transcaspian goods. Raw cotton, silk, and rice pass through. Population leapt from 13,381 in 1860. By 1900 it reached 179,133.
britannica-1911-bangor-co-down:
Bangor is a seaport and market town of County Down, Ireland, on the south side of Belfast Lough, twelve miles east of Belfast by rail. Its urban district held 5,903 people in 1901. Trade in cotton, linen, and embroidered muslin went on in the town.

Bangor was much used as a watering place, above all by the people of Belfast, and it had golf links and regattas run by the Royal Ulster Yacht Club. Slight remains survive of its abbey of Canons Regular, founded in the mid 500s by St Comgall and rebuilt grandly by St Malachy in the 1100s. The 1911 Britannica entry closes by noting the town's incorporation by James I and its two members in the old Irish parliament.
britannica-1911-battle-town:
Battle is a market-town in Sussex, England, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in a pleasant, rolling, well-wooded district, seven miles from the sea at Hastings, and its district held 2996 people in 1901. The town takes its name from the great fight of 1066, in which William the Norman beat King Harold and won the crown of England. Before that fight William swore to build an abbey on the spot if he won, and the abbey church was blessed with great pomp in 1094.

Stone traces carry the long tale. The abbey gatehouse, a work in the Decorated style, ends the town's main street in fine form. Parts remain of the Norman church's base, the cloisters, and the refectory, the monks' dining hall. A mansion now stands on part of the site and folds some of the old building into itself.
britannica-1911-belfort-town:
Belfort is a town of eastern France on the Savoureuse river, 275 miles east-south-east of Paris. It is capital of the Territory of Belfort and a rail crossroads for Basel, Lyons, Mülhausen and Strassburg. The river splits an old fortified quarter, with the castle, from a newer one holding the station.

Two monuments recall the siege of 1870–1871: Bartholdi’s huge “Lion of Belfort” before the castle and Mercié’s “Quand Même” group. Belfort stayed French after that war and grew into a key frontier fortress. Its history runs from Gallo-Roman finds through two sieges in the Thirty Years’ War to Denfert-Rochereau’s famed defence of 1870–1871.
britannica-1911-blois-town:
Blois, a town of central France, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the department of Loir et Cher, thirty five miles south west of Orleans. It stands on the right bank of the Loire, in a thickly wooded district. The entry gives it 18,457 people in 1906.

Blois covers the tops and slopes of two hills, with its main street in the dip between them. An eighteenth century bridge joins it to the suburb of Vienne across the river. From the bridge the town looks like an amphitheatre. The streets of the older, higher part are narrow, winding, and so steep that flights of steps serve as climbs. Its famed chateau of the Orleans family stands on the western hill. The north west wing, built by Francis the First, holds the room where the duke of Guise was murdered.
britannica-1911-bordentown:
Bordentown is a small city in Burlington county, New Jersey, on the east bank of the Delaware River, 6 miles south of Trenton and 28 miles north-east of Philadelphia. Its people hovered near 4200 across the counts of 1890 to 1910. Railways, an electric line toward New York, and river steamboats all served it.

The city sits on a broad plain 65 feet above the river, with wide, well-shaded streets. It housed the Bordentown Military Institute, a state training school for coloured youth, and a convent and girls' academy of the Sisters of Mercy. Ship yards, iron foundries, machine shops, shirt and pottery works, and canning factories are listed. Quaker families settled the site in the 1700s, and Joseph Borden laid out the town that bears his name.
britannica-1911-cape-town:
Cape Town, the capital of the Cape Province in South Africa, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies at the north-west tip of the Cape Peninsula, on the south shore of Table Bay. It is more than six thousand miles by sea from London. The entry opens with praise for its setting, calling few cities more grandly placed.

Behind the bay the flat wall of Table Mountain rises more than 3,500 feet, two miles long. Mountains close the plain on the east and west, among them the Devil's Peak and the Lion's Head. The city first clung to the land at the head of the bay, then spread round its shores and up the lower slopes. The Dutch look it kept until the middle of the last century had gone. Brick houses with flat roofs and wide porches had given way to shops and offices.
britannica-1911-carlow-town:
Carlow is the county town of county Carlow, Ireland. It stands on the navigable river Barrow. It lies 56 miles south-west of Dublin by rail. Its urban district held 6513 people in 1901. This 1911 Britannica entry describes the town. The castle stands on an eminence over the river. It is still a chief feature of the town's view.

Little of the original castle building remains today. It was a hollow quadrangle with four round towers. The principal buildings include St Patrick's Roman Catholic College. It dates from 1793 and stands in a picturesque park. The Catholic cathedral of Kildare and Leighlin adjoins it. The court-house is an octagonal stone building. Its handsome Ionic portico fronts the assizes court. Wellington Bridge links the town to its suburb of Graigue. A fine cromlech stands two miles north-east of the town.
britannica-1911-carpi-town:
Carpi is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and episcopal see in Emilia, Italy, in the province of Modena. It stands nine miles north-north-west of Modena by rail, and its population in 1905 was 7118 in the town and 27,135 in the commune. The town serves as a rail junction and as the centre of a fertile farming district.

Nearly every main building is built of the local marble. The old cathedral began as an early Romanesque church and holds frescoes from the early fifteenth century, while the new cathedral dates from after 1513. The entry credits Alberto Pio of Carpi, a pupil of Aldus Manutius, with these buildings and the town walls. Charles V drove him out in 1525 and gave the principality to the house of Este. The prince's palace, with its court and chapel frescoes by Bernardino Loschi, also gets a mention.
britannica-1911-carrara-town:
Carrara is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Tuscany, Italy, in the province of Massa e Carrara, 390 feet above sea level. Its people numbered 38,100 in the town and 48,493 in the commune in 1905. The cathedral, built between 1272 and 1385, is a fine Gothic work from the days of Pisan rule. Nearly every chief building in town is made of the local marble, the source of Carrara's fame.

Some quarries were worked in Roman times, then lay idle until Pisan building in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries revived demand. By the entry's time the quarries spread across almost the whole Apuan Alps, with about 600 in work. Of these, 345 at Carrara itself employed 4400 men, and exports in 1899 reached 180,000 tons. A separate railway served the quarries. The academy in town holds Roman finds from the pits and modern work by local sculptors.
britannica-1911-castellon-de-la-plana-to:
Castellon de la Plana is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a town in Spain. It is the capital of the province of the same name. The town stands on the main rail line between Barcelona and Valencia, four miles from the sea. The hosted text reaches the town article after the tail of the province article.

The article gives the town count as 29,904 in the year 1900. A broad, rich plain spreads around it, watered by an old Moorish channel cut through rock. Old walls still ring part of the town. Sights named include convents, a tall bell tower, and a church with a work by the painter Ribalta. Trade is brisk in china ware, leather, silk, linen, brandy, and cork goods. Orange groves fill the land to the south west.
britannica-1911-chernigov-town:
Chernigov is a town of Russia and capital of the government of that name, set on the right bank of the Desna, 141 miles by rail north-east of Kiev. Its people numbered 27,006 in 1897, and it is an archiepiscopal see. The town has a cathedral from the 11th century. A branch rail line serves it, and it stands nearly half a mile from the river.

In 907 the city appears in the treaty of Oleg as next in importance to Kiev, the entry notes. In the 11th century it became capital of the principality of Syeversk and a busy trading city. The Mongol invasion ended its prosperity in 1239. Lithuania, then Poland, held it in later centuries, and in 1686 it was finally annexed to Russia.
britannica-1911-clown:
Clown names first a rustic, boorish person, and then the comic character in English pantomime, always in baggy costume with whitened, eccentrically painted face and a tufted wig. Fuller derived the word from the Latin colonus, a husbandman, in his Worthies. The entry instead links it apparently with clod and with similar forms in Teutonic and Scandinavian languages. That earthy root suits the rustic sense better than Fuller's guess in the account given.

The character probably descends from representations of the devil in medieval miracle plays, the entry argues. It developed partly through stage rustics and partly through the fools or jesters, also called clowns, of Elizabethan drama. Whitened face and baggy costume indicate a connexion also with the continental Pierrot figure. Prominence of the clown in pantomime is a comparatively modern development beside that of Harlequin, whose stage history runs much longer.
britannica-1911-cochin-town:
Cochin was a town of British India in the Malabar district of Madras, with 19,274 people in 1901. It stood at the north end of a narrow strip of land about twelve miles long. Sea inlets and streams from the Western Ghats nearly cut that strip off. Behind the shore lay the shallow Cochin backwaters.

Those backwaters shaped town life. In the monsoon they became broad channels fit for boats. In hot weather they shrank to shallows under two feet deep. The entry traces rule by the Portuguese, Dutch and British in turn. Vasco da Gama set up a factory in 1502. A fort followed in 1503. Trade in coconut goods and tea still went on, and large ships could be built there.
britannica-1911-creetown: Creetown, a seaport in Kirkcudbrightshire, Scotland, is the subject of a brief 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands near the head of Wigtown Bay, west of Castle Douglas. In nineteen oh one it had just under one thousand folk. Granite quarries nearby form the chief trade. Stone from them went into the Liverpool docks and other large works. The village dates from seventeen eighty five. Walter Scott set part of his novel Guy Mannering in the area nearby.
britannica-1911-crown:
Crown, as an English coin, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The crown is a silver coin worth five shillings, and the word is often used for that sum of money. The first crowns were of gold and were struck in the reign of Henry the Eighth. Silver crowns and half-crowns came in under Edward the Sixth.

Down to the reign of Charles the Second, crowns and half-crowns, and at times double crowns, were struck in gold and in silver both. The habit of dating coins and of marking their worth on them also began under Edward the Sixth. Since Charles the Second the crown has been struck in silver alone. In the nineteenth century it was near dropped. None was made from 1861 to 1887, but since the new issue of 1887 it has been in free use once more.
britannica-1911-dan-town:
Dan was a town of ancient Israel near the head-waters of the Jordan. Before the Danites took it, a peaceful trading people held it and called it Laish or Leshem. Even then it seems to have been a holy place, for Micah's shrine was moved there. Jeroboam chose it as the site of one of his calf-shrines. Dan names the north limit of Palestine in the saying, from Dan to Beersheba.

Benhadad of Damascus plundered the town, and from that blow it seems to have declined by slow degrees. Scholars seek its site in the mound called Tell-el-Kadi, the hill of the judge, since Dan means judge in Hebrew. Weighty authorities place it instead four miles east, at Banias, the old Caesarea Philippi. The entry leaves that quarrel open. Shrine, proverb, plunder, and a disputed mound make up its whole account of the place.
britannica-1911-elisavetpol-town:
Elisavetpol, formerly Ganja, was a town of Russia and capital of the government of the same name, lying 118 miles by rail south-east of Tiflis at 1446 feet. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the town article within it. Its population was 15,439 in 1873 and 33,090 in 1897. The town is very old, and the Russians took it in 1804.

Persians, Khazars, and Arabs held the town even in the 7th century, and Mongols, Georgians, Persians, and Turks held it later in turn. The entry calls it a badly built place of narrow streets and low-roofed, windowless houses in an unhealthy spot. A new European quarter has risen on the old fortress site. Its people, chiefly Tatars and Armenians, are famed for gardening and silkworm breeding. A mosque built by Shah Abbas of Persia in 1620 still stands, and the poet Shah Nizam was born here in 1141.
britannica-1911-elster-town:
Elster is a spa and inland watering-place of Germany in the kingdom of Saxony, on the Weisse Elster near the Bohemian frontier, 20 miles south of Plauen on the railway to Eger. It has some lace-making and weaving, and a population of about 2000 besides its visitors. The place serves as a climatic health resort in summer. About 10,000 visitors come each year.

The mineral springs are saline-chalybeate, that is, salt and iron bearing, and are held specific for nervous disorders and women's ailments. Baths of various kinds have lately been added to the springs. Those baths, with the natural charms of the place, have made Elster a fashionable watering-place in the summer season. The entry closes by pointing readers to Flechsig's Bad Elster, printed at Leipzig in 1884. The picture is of a small Saxon town whose whole life turns on its healing waters and its summer guests.
britannica-1911-ems-town:
Ems is a town and watering-place of Germany in the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. It stands on both banks of the Lahn in a valley ringed by wooded mountains and vine-clad hills, eleven miles east from Coblenz. The hosted file holds several articles together; this entry is the town article within it. Its population is given as 6500. The town has five churches, among them English and Russian ones, and some silver and lead mining.

Ems ranks among the most fashionable watering-places of Europe, drawing about 11,000 visitors a year. Its waters are some twenty hot alkaline springs, used for drinking and bathing, and held good for nervous disorders, liver complaints, and chest troubles. A stone on the promenade marks the spot where, on 13 July 1870, King William of Prussia held his famous meeting with the French ambassador, Count Benedetti.
britannica-1911-este-town:
Este, known in old times as Ateste, is a town and bishop's see in Venetia, Italy, in the province of Padua. It lies some twenty miles south-west of Padua by rail, below the south slopes of the Euganean Hills. The town had 8,671 people in 1901. The walls of its castle still stand above the town, but the inside now holds a cattle market. A part of the old Mocenigo palace holds a rich museum of finds.

The town church was built from 1690 to 1720 on the site of one lost in a quake in 1688. After Roman times the record goes blank until the Lombard age. In the tenth century the house of Este set itself up in the castle. Padua took the town for good by the end of the thirteenth century.
britannica-1911-farah-town:
Farah, a town of Afghanistan, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river of the same name, on the main road between Herat and Kandahar. It lies 160 miles south of Herat and 225 miles west of Kandahar, at 2,460 feet above the sea. Its spot gave it weight in war, since it commands the roads toward India and Seistan from Herat.

The article describes a square walled town in the middle of a plain, ringed by a rampart. Ill health had left it almost empty, held only by the Afghan regiment posted there. It was a place of great age, most likely the Phra named by a writer of the first century. Sacked by the armies of Jenghiz Khan and besieged in later years, it had shrunk much, and its sole trade was the making of gunpowder.
britannica-1911-faro-town:
Faro is the capital of its district in southern Portugal, at the end of the Lisbon railway on the Atlantic. Its 1900 population was 11,789. It is an episcopal see with a large Renaissance cathedral, a seminary, and a ruined castle ringed by Moorish walls. The harbour is broad but shallow, guarded by the long island of Cães. Silt from the river Fermoso keeps enlarging the sandy islets, and large vessels cannot enter.

Fishing matters most, and fish, wine, fruit, cork, baskets and sumach lead the exports. The district's tin, lead, antimony and gold-bearing quartz remain little worked. Alphonso III took Faro from the Moors in his reign, 1248 to 1279. The English sacked it in 1596, and the earthquake of 1755 nearly destroyed it. Its district matches the old province of Algarve, with 255,191 people over 1,937 square miles.
britannica-1911-galway-town:
Galway is a seaport and county town in the west of Ireland, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it in detail. The town stands on the north shore of Galway Bay, on the Midland Great Western railway line. Its urban district held 13,426 people in 1901. Some streets are very narrow and hold odd old houses in a Spanish style.

The best known of these houses is Lynch’s Castle, named for a leading town family. A tale told of Mayor James Lynch Fitzstephen says he hanged his own son in 1493 for a crime. Some link that stern act to the start of the term Lynch law. The entry also notes St Nicholas church, a cross shaped building founded in 1320. The church was made collegiate in 1484 and holds old monuments.
britannica-1911-gown:
Gown is the subject of a dress entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word properly names a loose outer garment once worn by either sex. By the time of the entry it was used chiefly for women's dress. In American use gown was the common word where English speakers said dress.

The entry traces the word to Old French forms and to a medieval Latin word. That Latin word was used of a garment of skin or fur. A Celtic source has often been claimed for the word. The entry notes that the Irish and Gaelic forms were in fact taken from English. Special robes for office and study are also covered.
britannica-1911-graham-s-town:
Graham’s Town is a city of South Africa, and a centre for the eastern Cape province, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica paints the place. It lies 106 miles by rail north east of Port Elizabeth. Its count in 1904 came to 13,887 people. Of those, 7,283 were whites and 1,837 were electors.

The town is built in a basin of grassy hills, spurs of the Zuurberg. It stands 1,760 feet above the sea in that basin. The entry calls it a pleasant place to live. Its climate is held to be markedly healthy. It is regarded as the most English like town in the Cape. Broad streets, most of them lined with trees, mark its plan. In the High Street stand the law courts and the Anglican cathedral of St George. That church was built from designs by Sir Gilbert Scott.
britannica-1911-grantown:
Grantown, the capital of Speyside in Elginshire, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies on the left bank of the Spey, south of Forres by rail. In nineteen oh one it had just over fifteen hundred folk. Two rail lines serve the town.

It was founded in seventeen seventy six by Sir James Grant. The Grant family had lived on a nearby estate since the early fourteen hundreds. Public buildings include a town hall, a court house, and an orphan hospital. Trade rests on cattle and on whisky making. The town is built of grey granite and looks handsome. Pine and birch woods, pure air, and a bracing climate draw guests.
britannica-1911-greytown:
Greytown, or San Juan del Norte, is the principal seaport on the Caribbean coast of Nicaragua, at the mouth of the San Juan river. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it about 2,500 people in 1905. The town stands on a narrow peninsula, its houses raised on piles two or three feet above the ground.

The neighbourhood is unhealthy and grows almost nothing, so food is imported and living dear. The port's story is one of silting. Between 1850 and 1875 the depth over its bar fell from about 25 feet to five, and the entrance nearly closed. Dredging and jetties had only partial success, yet Greytown stayed the headquarters of Nicaraguan trade with Europe and America. The entry recalls its history: port of entry in 1796, seized under the British Mosquito protectorate in 1848, and ceded back to Nicaragua by the treaty of Managua in 1860.
britannica-1911-groningen-town:
Groningen, capital of the Dutch province of the same name, stands where the canalised Drentsche Aa and Hunse meet, 33 miles east of Leeuwarden by rail. Its population in 1900 was 67,563. Canals radiate from the town to Delfzyl, Leeuwarden, Assen and the Ems, making it the leading town of the north of Holland.

The Groote Markt is one of Holland's largest market squares, and the Martini-kerk's tower of 1477 rises 432 feet, its organ built by the scholar Rudolph Agricolo. The university, founded in 1614, anchors the town's institutions alongside a museum of antiquities, a deaf and dumb institution dating from 1790, and learned societies for law and natural science. A closing history runs from the medieval town through siege and French occupation to the demolition of its fortifications after 1874.
britannica-1911-irkutsk-town:
Irkutsk, chief town of its government, is presented in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as the most weighty place in Siberia. It is the largest hub of people there and the main depot of trade north of Tashkent. It is also a walled army post and an archbishopric of the Orthodox Greek Church. Learned societies make their seat in the town as well.

The town lies 3792 miles by rail from St Petersburg. Its people grew from 32512 in 1875 to 49106 in 1900. The town proper stands on the right bank of the Angara, a stream that feeds the Yenisei. Lake Baikal feeds that river forty five miles above the town. A flying bridge crosses the broad stream to the suburb on the far bank. The small Irkut river, source of the town name, joins the Angara just opposite.
britannica-1911-kaluga-town:
Kaluga is the chief town of the government of the same name, on the left bank of the Oka, 117 miles southwest of Moscow by rail. Its people numbered 36,880 in 1870 and 49,728 in 1897. It is the seat of a Greek Orthodox bishop. Its public buildings include the Trinity cathedral, rebuilt in the 19th century, two monasteries, a seminary, and a lunatic asylum.

Its chief products are leather, oil, bast mats, wax candles, starch, and Kaluga cakes. The town is first named in history in 1389 and was joined to the principality of Moscow in 1518. In 1607 the second false Demetrius held it against a four month siege. In 1619 it fell to the Zaporozhian Cossacks, plague later carried off two thirds of its people, and in 1622 fire laid the whole place waste. It rose again despite fresh fires, among them those of 1742 and 1754, and at times it housed exiled Polish princes.
britannica-1911-kazan-town:
Kazan, called Ozon by the Cheremisses, is a town of eastern Russia, capital of the government of the same name. It stands on the river Kazanka, 3 miles from the Volga, though the great river reaches the city when it floods each spring. It lies 650 miles east of Moscow by rail. Its people numbered 140,726 in 1883 and 143,707 in 1900, all Russians save some 20,000 Tatars.

The most striking feature of the city is the kreml, or citadel, founded in 1437, which crowns a low hill in the northwest. Inside its wall, capped with five towers, stand several churches. Among them is the cathedral of the Annunciation, founded in 1562 by Gury, the first archbishop of Kazan. The kreml also holds a great monastery built in 1556, an arsenal, the governor's castle, and the red brick Suyumbeka tower, 246 feet high. The long entry gives the city its full gazetteer due.
britannica-1911-kerman-town:
Kerman is the capital of the Persian province of the same name, standing at an elevation of 6100 feet. Its people are put at 60,000, including about 2000 Zoroastrians, 100 Jews, and a few Shikarpuri Indians. The town has post and telegraph offices of the Indo European Telegraph Department, British and Russian consulates, and an agency of the Imperial bank of Persia.

The districts round it grow little grain and must bring in supplies for four or five months of the year from far away. In 1879 the authorities told Sir A. Houtum Schindler to cut short his travels in the province because his horses and mules were eating up all the stock. Kerman makes great quantities of carpets and felts, and its carpets are almost without match for richness of weave and lasting wear.
britannica-1911-kingstown:
Kingstown is a seaport in County Dublin, Ireland, and a gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the town. It stands at the south east end of Dublin Bay, six miles from Dublin by rail. Its urban district held 17,377 people in 1901. The town is a large seaport and a favoured seaside resort.

Fine streets, electric trams, and terraces with wide sea views mark the town. Its first name was Dunleary, the entry notes. The name changed after George the Fourth embarked at the port in 1821. He was then on his way back from Ireland. An obelisk of granite near the harbour marks that event. Before its great harbour was built, Kingstown was a mere fishing village. The harbour works began in 1817.
britannica-1911-kursk-town:
Kursk is a town of Russia, capital of the government of the same name. It stands where the railways from Moscow, Kiev and Kharkov meet, 330 miles S.S.W. from Moscow. In 1897 it held 52,896 people. The town is built on two hills of 750 feet, their slopes planted with orchards, and the woods around it are famed for their nightingales. Its noted buildings include a monastery with an image of the Virgin honoured since 1295, and Kursk is a bishopric and the birthplace of the saint Theodosius.

Kursk has mills, distilleries, tobacco works, tanneries, soap works and iron works, and a great yearly fair, the Korennaya. Its trade covers grain, linen, leather, horses, cattle, furs, wax and tallow. The town stood already in 1032. The Mongols destroyed it wholly in 1240. Its defence against the Polovtsi is sung in The Triumph of Igor, a prized relic of early Russian letters.
britannica-1911-kutais-town:
Kutais is a town of Russian Caucasia, capital of the government of the same name. It stands 60 miles by rail E. of Poti, and in 1897 held 32,492 people. It is one of the oldest towns of Caucasia. It was Aea or Kutaea, the ancient capital of Colchis, and from 792 the capital of Imeretia. Persians, Mongols, Turks and Russians have destroyed it again and again. In 1810 it became Russian. The town lies on both banks of the Rion, crossed by three bridges.

Its chief sight is its ruined cathedral. The Bagratids, the ruling house of Georgia, built it in the 11th century, and the Turks destroyed it in 1692. It is the finest relic of Georgian building still standing. The old fort is also a heap of ruins. The people make hats and silks, and trade in farm produce and wine.
britannica-1911-marshalltown:
Marshalltown is a city in Marshall County, Iowa, near the Iowa river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it north east of Des Moines. Its people grew to over thirteen thousand by 1910. Three rail lines served it, one with machine shops in town.

A soldiers home and a Catholic business school were based there. Rich farm land made the city a market for grain and stock. Meat cattle, horses, and swine passed through its yards in trade. Factories added goods worth over three million dollars in 1905. The town was laid out in 1853 and named for Chief Justice John Marshall.
britannica-1911-maxwelltown:
Maxwelltown, a burgh in Kirkcudbrightshire in Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the river Nith, across from Dumfries. Three bridges join the two towns, and they vote as one for parliament. The count in 1901 was 5796 people.

A court house, the prison for the south west of Scotland, and a museum in an old windmill mark its public stock. Woollens and hosiery are its chief goods, with dye works and sawmills beside them. Till 1810 it was a hamlet called Bridgend. That year it became a burgh under its present name. Near it stands the fine ruin of Lincluden Abbey in the parish of Terregles.
britannica-1911-meissen-town:
Meissen is a town of Germany in the kingdom of Saxony state. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on both banks of the Elbe, north west of Dresden city. Counts from nineteen o five put its people at just over thirty two thousand.

The old town lies on the left bank, on a hilly uneven site. Narrow streets and many fine old buildings make the town scenic. The cathedral, a fine early Gothic work, crowns the Schlossberg hill. Building began in the thirteenth century and ended about fourteen fifty. Tombs of Saxon rulers, plus works by Vischer and Cranach, fill it.
britannica-1911-montmorency-town:
Montmorency is a town of northern France in the Seine et Oise district. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands eleven miles north of Paris by rail, near the Seine river. In the middle ages it was the seat of the Montmorency family.

A church built mostly in the sixteenth century by Anne de Montmorency stands there. The town is a well known resort for people from Paris. A fine forest of the same name lies to the north east. Work in the town covers bleach and dye shops and lime plaster. Brick and tile making are also carried on in the town.
britannica-1911-morgantown:
Morgantown, a city in West Virginia, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is the county seat of Monongalia county and stands on the Monongahela river. The river can be sailed as far as Fairmont, above the city. Morgantown lies about 50 miles south-east of Wheeling. Its people numbered 9,150 in the 1910 census, up from 1,895 in 1900.

The city is the seat of West Virginia University, which grew from an academy founded in 1814 and a female seminary from 1858. The school was chartered in 1867 and took its present name in 1868. In 1908 it had 80 instructors and 1,534 students. Coal, glass-sand, and limestone are found near the city. The first settlement was made about 1768 by David and Zackwill Morgan. The town took its name from the latter and became a city in 1905.
britannica-1911-morristown:
Morristown, the county seat of Morris County in New Jersey, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It stands on the Whippany River, thirty one miles west of New York City by rail. Its count rose from 8,156 in 1890 to 12,507 in 1910. The town sits on high flat land ringed by fine hills.

Morristown is chiefly a home suburb of New York, with many large estates. It was settled near 1710 by Puritans drawn by iron ore. Washington's army camped there in two hard war winters. At its old Speedwell iron works, part of the first ship to cross the Atlantic by steam was made. Morse and Vail also finished the electric wire message tool there.
britannica-1911-neuchatel-town:
Neuchâtel, a Swiss lake town, is laid out in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands near the north-east corner of its own lake. Rail lines meet there from Bern, Bienne, France, and Yverdon. The station sits high, joined to the shore by an electric tram. Old streets climb the steep slope of the Chaumont hill.

Lake waters once washed the foot of that old town hill. Silt and new bank work have since added dry land. Fine new blocks now rise on that made ground by the quays. The old castle and the church of Notre Dame stand close by. Both trace to the twelfth century, when counts settled in town. A charter of freedoms came to the town in 1214.
britannica-1911-orenburg-town:
Orenburg is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Orenburg is a town of Russia on the Ural River. It was the capital of the government of the same name. Rail lines linked it with Samara and, from 1905, with distant Tashkent.

The entry stresses the town's role in trade. It was the seat of an Orthodox bishop and of the Orenburg Cossack host. Three miles away stood a barter house where camel caravans arrived from Central Asia. They brought carpets, silks, cottons, lambskins, and dried fruits. In exchange they took Russian cloth, metal goods, and sugar. Huge numbers of horses, cattle, and sheep changed hands there each year. The article gives a clear picture of a frontier town where Europe met the steppe.
britannica-1911-paton-john-brown:
John Brown Paton (born 1830) was a British Nonconformist divine, and a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica records his training and posts. He was born on the seventeenth of December 1830. He was educated in London, at Poole, and at Spring Hill College in Birmingham. He took his first degree at London University in 1849.

Paton won prizes in Hebrew and the New Testament in 1850. In 1854 he took a gold medal in philosophy. Glasgow University gave him an honorary doctorate in divinity in 1881. When the Nottingham Congregational Institute was founded in 1863, Paton became its first principal. He held that post until 1898, a span of thirty five years. In 1907 he became vice president of the British and Foreign Bible Society.
britannica-1911-penza-town:
Penza (town) is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Russian provincial capital. Penza stands 492 miles by rail south east of Moscow, on a plateau 567 feet above the sea, where the Penza river meets the navigable Sura. Its population in 1897 was 61,851. The older parts of the town are built of wood, but the newer parts are well built. Its cathedral dates from 1820 to 1821.

The article lists the town's institutions and trades. Penza has technical schools, libraries, a museum, and a theatre of note in Russian stage history. Most inhabitants live by farming or by fishing in the Sura. An imperial botanical garden stands within two miles. Apart from paper mills and steam flour mills, its factories are small.
britannica-1911-perm-town:
Perm, a town of Russia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of the government of the same name. The town stands on the left bank of the Kama, on the great highway to Siberia. The census of 1897 counted 45,403 people there.

In summer, steamers link Perm with Kazan, six hundred miles away. A railway runs east to Ekaterinburg, across the Ural mountains. The town is mostly built of wood, with broad streets and wide squares. Perm is the seat of an Orthodox bishop and holds a seminary and schools. Its industries grow slowly, led by shipyards, tanneries, and sawmills. The state keeps a great gun and munitions works nearby. A copper works of 1723 first fixed the site in importance.
britannica-1911-poltava-town:
Poltava, a town in Russia on the Vorskla river, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of its government and lies west of Kharkov by rail. About fifty three thousand people lived there. The town stands on a plateau with steep slopes on near every side.

Cossack suburbs full of gardens ring the town, with a German colony as well. Its oldest sites are a monastery from 1650 and a wooden church. Peter the Great went to that church after his great battle nearby. Schools include a cadet school and a seminary for clergy. Mills, tobacco works, and a tannery support the town. Poltava is famed most for the battle of June 1709. There Peter beat Charles the Twelfth of Sweden, a win marked by a tall column.
britannica-1911-prome-town:
Prome was the chief town of its district in Burma, set on the left bank of the Irrawaddy river. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its place, about one hundred and sixty one miles north of Rangoon, and its town count from the census of that time. Low hills topped with pagodas close in the town on two sides, and one hill holds a famed gilded shrine.

Inside, the entry tells a short town history in plain facts. British troops took Prome twice with little fight, fire gutted it, and it was then laid out anew with straight broad streets. Later notes cover town rule, new waterworks, silk cloth and lacquer ware made there, and the rail line from Rangoon that ends in the town.
britannica-1911-roscommon-town:
Roscommon, a market town and the county town of County Roscommon in Ireland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on rising ground in a bare plain at the centre of the county, on a railway line, with 1,891 people in 1901. The town holds the county buildings and churches of both main faiths, the Catholic one a fine building finished in 1903.

An extensive trade is carried on in farm produce and livestock. A castle founded in 1268 by John d'Ufford, the justiciary of Ireland, overlooks the plain as an imposing mass of ruins, far gone in decay. It fell to besiegers in 1566, in 1642 and in 1652, and was partly burned after the battle of Aughrim in 1691. Remains of a Dominican priory also survive. The town's name means Saint Coman's wood, from the saint who founded a monastery there in the five hundreds.
britannica-1911-ryazan-town:
Ryazan is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Russian town that heads the government of the same name. The town stands 124 miles by rail south east of Moscow on the high bank of the Trubezh, above its meeting with the Oka, and held 44,552 people in 1897. Ryazan is the seat of an Orthodox archbishop.

The article untangles the town from its older namesake: Old Ryazan, near Spask, was the first capital of the principality, named in annals as early as 1097. In the eleventh century a Kiev prince founded a fort called Pereyaslav-Ryazanskiy, and in time the bishop and then the princes of Ryazan moved there, leaving the old town behind. Tatars plundered and burned it in 1365 and 1377, and a kreml stood on its crag into the seventeenth century.
britannica-1911-santander-town:
Santander is a seaport and capital city in northern Spain, on its bay. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on a rocky point that guards a fine harbor. Its people passed fifty four thousand in 1900 by the count. Rail lines from Valladolid and Bilbao end at its port in trade.

Upper and lower towns split the city by height on the point. A Gothic cathedral holds a crypt with a Moorish font of note. A dynamite ship blast in 1893 wrecked much of the bay front. Rebuilding and harbor works drove growth in the late century that followed. Trade rights with America dated from 1753 for the port.
britannica-1911-schaffhausen-town:
Schaffhausen is the capital town of the Swiss canton of the same name on the Rhine. A 1911 Britannica entry sets it on rising ground above the right bank of the river. Narrow streets mark the old quarters while new parts spread wider in plan. The fortress of Unnoth looks down over the roofs of the town.

Old Swabian houses mix with modern factories in a curious blend of ages. Three of the old sixteen town gates still stand in the streets. The chief old building is the Munster of All Saints, once a Benedictine house. Consecrated in 1052, it shows the plainest Romanesque style with one side tower.
britannica-1911-schwyz-town:
Schwyz is the capital of the Swiss canton of the same name, a small town in a fine setting. It stands amid fruit trees on a mountain terrace, at a height of about seventeen hundred feet. The conical peak of the Gross Mythen rises at its north west foot. Below it lies the valley of the Muota river. The town holds a stately church of the eighteenth century and several convents.

A town hall of the sixteenth century keeps old papers and banners won in war. Old patrician houses stand in the town, among them that of the Reding family. One Reding led the stand against the French in seventeen ninety eight. The parish held about seven thousand four hundred people in nineteen hundred. Near all spoke German and were Roman Catholic in faith.
britannica-1911-simon-s-town:
Simon's Town is a port and naval base in the Cape province of South Africa. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on Simon's Bay off False Bay. It lies 17 miles north of Cape Point by the coast road. A rail line links it with Cape Town to the north. Its count in 1904 was 6,642 souls, the entry notes.

Apart from the base, the town draws schools and homes of rest. Its mild air is praised, with warm days and cool nights year round. Warm seas in the bay make it a loved spot for bathing. The naval yard forms the head base for the Cape squadron. In 1900 the yard spread across some thirteen acres of ground.
britannica-1911-sligo-town:
Sligo, a port and market town in Ireland, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It is the county town of county Sligo. Its people numbered 10,870 in 1901. The town stands at the head of an arm of Sligo Bay. It lies on the river Garvogue, north-west of Dublin. Three railways meet at the junction south of the town.

The article praises the town's fine setting by Lough Gill. Sligo ranks with Galway and Limerick among the chief west-coast ports. Steamers run to Liverpool and Glasgow on a regular basis. Exports include grain, flour, pork, and cattle. Coal, iron, and timber come in by sea. Brewing, flour milling, and saw milling are the chief trades. The Dominican Abbey, founded in 1252, is called one of the finest ruins in Ireland.
britannica-1911-smolensk-town:
Smolensk is a Russian town on the Dnieper River. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls it one of the oldest towns of Russia. Rail lines from Moscow, Riga, and Orel meet there. Its count at the turn of the century topped fifty-seven thousand.

The town climbs high crags on the left bank. Walls from the reign of Boris Godunov ring its old citadel. A cathedral raised over a hundred years holds a famed icon. That image of the Virgin draws honor across central Russia. Three public libraries and a museum serve the town now. Smolensk was chief town of a Slav tribe in old chronicles. It traded down the great route to Constantinople for centuries. Poland and Russia fought over it again and again.
britannica-1911-soleure-town:
Soleure, a small old Swiss town, is drawn in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands most of it on the left bank of the Aar. Rome set a fort there on the road from Avenches to Basel. Its place at the foot of the Jura drew roads to one point. Five rail lines branch from the town, with a new sixth by tunnel.

Walls raised in the late sixteen hundreds are long since gone. The town razed them from 1830 for room and ease of life. Its great church of Saints Ursus and Victor dates from the 1700s. Since 1828 it has served as the Basel bishop's own cathedral. A quaint clock of the sixteenth century marks the old tower. Its arsenal holds the finest old arms in all Switzerland.
britannica-1911-st-gall-town:
St Gall, capital of the Swiss canton of the same name, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The town stands in the upland valley of the Steinach, 2,195 feet above the sea. It lies nine miles by rail from Rorschach, its port on Lake Constance. Zurich is 53 miles to the west. The old centre keeps the air of a small rural capital, while newer quarters look modern.

The chief building is the abbey church of the famed old monastery, a cathedral since 1846. Its present form dates from 1756 to 1765. The abbey library, housed in the former abbot's palace, is renowned for its early manuscripts and printed books. Other monastery buildings hold the offices of the canton and its archives. The town owes its origin to St Gall, an Irish hermit who built his cell there in 614.
britannica-1911-stavropol-town:
Stavropol is a town of south Russia and capital of its province. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it on a plateau 2,030 feet high. It lies on the north slope of the Caucasus, far from Vladikavkaz. A rail line of 247 miles links it with Rostov on the Don. Founded in 1776, it has grown fast in a short span of time.

Its count rose from 35,561 in 1885 to 46,965 in 1900. The town is a see of the Orthodox Greek church in Russia. Wide streets and houses of stone give it a fine, built look. Large gardens ring those houses in the best provincial style. Trade in cattle, grain, tallow, and sheepskins fills its market life.
britannica-1911-stuart-james-ewell-brown:
Stuart, James Ewell Brown is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the Confederate cavalry general known to history as Jeb Stuart. Born in Virginia on the sixth of February 1833, he entered West Point in 1850 and took a cavalry commission in 1854. He saw much service in Indian warfare and in Kansas. In 1859 he helped Colonel Lee put down the John Brown raid on Harper's Ferry.

When Virginia seceded, Stuart resigned and was made a colonel, since cavalry officers were scarce. Raised to brigadier general, he led the cavalry brigade of the Army of Northern Virginia. Before the Seven Days' Battle, Lee sent him to find the flank of McClellan's army, and Stuart not only did the work but rode clean around the enemy rear to report.
britannica-1911-tlaxcala-town:
Tlaxcala, a town of Mexico, is the subject of a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of a state of the same name and stands on the Atoyac river. The town lies fifty eight miles east of Mexico City by rail. Its population in 1900 was 2,715, the entry gives.

Tlaxcala holds historic interest for its link with the conquest of Mexico by Cortes. The state house is its only fine building of a political kind. The old bishop's palace is its finest building of a religious kind. Of most interest, perhaps, is the church of San Francisco. The entry calls it the first church raised on the American continent. It still holds vestments, a pulpit, a font, and a cedar ceiling brought from Spain in 1521.
britannica-1911-town:
Town, in its most general sense, is a group of inhabited houses larger than a village, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. The old English word tun first meant a fence or an enclosure in its use. A sense much like hedge in German lies behind that first meaning. Scots and northern English use of town for a farmhouse and its buildings keeps that first sense alive.

A kindred Celtic form means a fastness or strong place, the text notes. It shows in Gaelic and Irish dun and in Welsh din for a fortress or hill fort. In English law town is not a word defined by statute at all. For local government there are boroughs, urban districts, and rural districts in its place. Many urban districts are rural in character, so the split is one of administration pure and simple.
britannica-1911-tulle-town:
Tulle is the subject of a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Tulle is a town of central France, capital of its department. It stands southeast of Limoges by rail, along a narrow river valley. Its people numbered near twelve thousand in the town at the census given. Tulle is the seat of a bishop.

The article describes its cathedral of the twelve hundreds, of which the porch and nave remain. Its choir and transept were destroyed in 1793, but a tower with a fine stone steeple stands. A restored cloister and an abbot's house with a carved doorway stand nearby. The town holds courts, schools, and a branch of the Bank of France. Its chief trade is the making of small arms, set up in 1690 and run by the state. At its busiest the factory employed three thousand hands.
britannica-1911-turkestan-town: Turkestan, also called Hazret, is named in a 1911 Britannica article as a town of Russian Turkestan. It lies in the province of Syr-darya, on the railway from Orenburg to Tashkent. Its people numbered 11,592 in 1897. The town stands near the Syr-darya river, at an altitude of 833 feet. It has a very old mosque of the saint Hazret-Yassavi. That shrine attracts many pilgrims. The town is a key depot for hides, wool, and other produce of cattle-breeding. The Russians captured it in 1864.
britannica-1911-tver-town:
Tver is a town of Russia and the capital of its own province. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it 104 miles north west of Moscow by rail. It stands on both banks of the Volga where the Tvertsa flows in. A floating bridge spans the great river at that point in town. Its count rose from 39,280 in 1885 to 45,644 in 1900.

The town is a seat of the Orthodox Greek church in Russia. Its oldest church dates from 1564, and its cathedral from 1689. A public garden now fills the site of the old fortress walls. Mills for cotton and flour lead the trade of the town. Glass works, sawmills, and yards for rail cars add to its work.
britannica-1911-uralsk-town:
Uralsk is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Asiatic Russia. It is capital of the province of the same name. It stands on the Ural river in that province. Counts show it grew from 26,055 in 1885 to 38,919 in 1901. It is rapidly developing in trade at that date. Its trade runs with the nomad Kirghiz of the steppe.

That trade deals in cattle, sheep, and animal products. All of those are exported onward to Russia. The town is also a centre for trade in grain. It has two cathedrals within its bounds. One was founded in the eighteenth century. The other dates from the year 1837. A small museum and a school farm stand in the town. A people's palace and free libraries are also named.
britannica-1911-usk-town:
Usk is a small market town set in fine country on the right bank of the river that bears its name. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its town count at the turn of the age as well under two thousand souls. It joins with two larger towns to send one member to the Commons.

The entry stresses the towns great age. It stands on the site of a Roman British town or fort. Fine ruins of an old castle stand there, built to guard the Welsh border lands. That post saw much strife from Norman times down to the days of a famed Welsh rebel chief. The church of the town first served a house of nuns of an old strict order.
britannica-1911-wexford-town:
Wexford, a sea port and county town in Ireland, fills a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It stands on the south side of the Slaney where that river meets its wide bay. Rail links run north to Dublin from its shore post. Its folk count for nineteen oh one was eleven thousand one hundred sixty eight. Long stone quays line the bay, but a sand bar bars deep ships at the mouth.

A new man made port at Rosslare opened in nineteen oh six to cure that bar. Old walls and towers still stand in part through the town. A church marks the spot of a peace made with English foes in eleven sixty nine. Farm goods, live stock, and whisky ship out from its quays. Ship build, tan, brew, and iron work fill its yards and shops.
britannica-1911-wigtown:
Wigtown, a royal burgh and the county town of Wigtownshire in Scotland, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the west shore of Wigtown Bay. Its name comes from a Norse word for bay. In 1901 it held a little over thirteen hundred people.

The town is built on a rise round a broad square laid out in walks. The entry notes the town hall, two old crosses, and a small fishing trade. Its most somber note is the fate of two women in 1685. Margaret MacLachlan and Margaret Wilson were tied to stakes in the bay sands and drowned by the tide. A tall stone raised in 1858 keeps their memory.
britannica-1911-zurich-town:
Zürich is the capital of the Swiss canton of the same name, and the largest town in Switzerland. The 1911 Britannica article calls it the most weighty and, on the whole, the finest town in the land. Till 1848 it served in fact as the capital of the Swiss Confederation. The town stands on both banks of the Limmat as it leaves the lake of Zürich. The Sihl stream joins the river just below the town.

The part on the right bank is called the Great Town, and that on the left the Little Town. In 1893 eleven outer districts were joined to the old city. Its count in 1900, with those districts, was 150,703, up from 35,483 in 1850. Land won from the lake holds fine quays and grand houses. The Bahnhofstrasse, from the station to the lake, holds the best shops in town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charlottetown:
Covering Prince Edward Island and the Magdalen Islands, the Diocese of Charlottetown takes its name from the island's chief town. Catholic history there begins in 1719, when the French king granted the Gulf islands to Count Saint-Pierre, and settlers soon gathered at Port La Joie. The first priests, Sulpicians René-Charles de Breslay and Marie-Anselme de Metivier, arrived in 1721, and Franciscans served the colony for thirty years after they left.

By 1753 five priests worked on the island, but the English invasion of 1758 drove most people out, razed the churches, and forced the clergy away. Recovery came slowly, above all under Peter MacIntyre, whose thirty-year rule from 1860 raised many churches and schools. By the early twentieth century the diocese held some fifty thousand Catholics under forty-five priests in fifty-one churches, with eight convents and St. Dunstan's College.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cooktown:
Henry Cleary's entry covers the Vicariate Apostolic of Cooktown, spanning North Queensland, Australia, from 16 degrees 30 minutes south latitude to Cape York. It reaches from the Pacific coast to the Northern Territory boundary. Formed out of the Diocese of Brisbane as a pro-vicariate in 1876, it was first entrusted to Italian priests, who subsequently withdrew. In 1882 it passed to the Irish Augustinians under Father John Hutchinson, pro-vicar. In 1887 the mission became a vicariate apostolic, with Dr. Hutchinson its first vicar.

He died on 28 October 1897, succeeded by the Right Reverend James D. Murray, consecrated 3 July 1898. Cairns serves as the vicariate's centre. Statistics to the close of 1907 list seven parish districts, 32 stations, 18 churches, eleven regular priests, 24 nuns, one boarding school, and three primary schools. 470 children attended Catholic schools, and the Catholic population stood about 6,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franciscan-cr:
The Franciscan Crown, also called the Seraphic Rosary, is a rosary of seven decades, or sets of ten prayers, in honour of the seven joys of the Blessed Virgin. They are the Annunciation, Visitation, Birth of the Lord, Adoration of the Magi, Finding of the Child in the Temple, Resurrection, and Assumption with her Coronation in heaven. It is used by members of the three orders of St. Francis, friars, nuns, and tertiaries alike.

The devotion dates to 1422. A young novice, who before entering had crowned a statue of Mary with fresh flowers, was tempted to leave because he could no longer keep that custom. The Virgin appeared, the story says, and taught him to weave a fairer crown by reciting seven decades daily for her joys, and the practice spread through the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-mi:
Richard of Middletown was a late thirteenth-century Franciscan schoolman whose life is mostly obscure but whose writings ranged widely. His birthplace is disputed, with two Oxfordshire and Northamptonshire villages proposed, and some claiming him as a Scotsman. He probably studied at Oxford, then graduated Bachelor of Divinity at Paris in 1283. His order twice set him to examine the doctrines of Peter Olivus.

In 1286 he travelled to Naples to tutor two sons of Charles II. When the princes were taken hostage to Barcelona, he shared their captivity until their release in 1295. His chief works include a commentary on the Sentences and his Quodlibeta, where he discusses what we would now call auto-suggestion and reports cases resembling telepathy. Many other works are ascribed to him, and several of those attributions are now judged false.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-visitatio:
Georgetown's Visitation Convent, in the District of Columbia, traces its roots here to an Irishwoman's voyage. Alice Lalor of Kilkenny sailed for America in 1794 with her sister Mrs Doran, wife of an American merchant. Aboard ship she grew close to Mrs Sharpe and Mrs McDermott, and united in vocation they bought a small Philadelphia house and began community life under Father Leonard Neale.

Yellow fever in 1797 and 1798 broke up their house, after earlier fever had killed Neale's predecessors Graessel and Fleming. Neale, now president of Georgetown College, invited them to settle there. Lalor bought a cottage near three French noblewomen of the Poor Clares, refugees from the Terror, and Neale placed the Pious Ladies under Saint Francis de Sales's rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-brown:
William Brown was an Irish-born sailor who became admiral of the Argentine navy and a founder of its republic. Born in County Mayo in 1777, he died at Buenos Aires. His family sailed for America in 1786, and he shipped as a cabin boy from Philadelphia. A French privateer took his English merchant ship, he escaped to England, married in 1809, and later wrecked his own trading vessel off South America.

There he ran the first regular packet line between Buenos Aires and Montevideo. In February 1814 the Buenos Aires rebels gave him seven ships. On Saint Patrick's Day he stormed the Martin Garcia fort, the Gibraltar of the La Plata, driving off nine Spanish warships. Montevideo fell in June, he took admiral's rank, and his 1827 victory at Juncal, seven ships against seventeen, broke the Brazilian blockade and sealed his fame.
darkness-and-dawn:
George Allan England's Darkness and Dawn is a trilogy of scientific romance, dedicated to Robert H. Davis, unique inspirer of plots. The first book, The Vacant World, opens with an awakening in a city of death, where two survivors face a world emptied of people.

Chapters follow exploration, treasure-trove, a sign of peril, a thousand years, the gathering of hordes, and the fight in the forest. Later books, Beyond the Great Oblivion and the closing volume, trace settling down, a golden age, deadly peril, and the rebirth of civilisation. Readers who enjoy early post-apocalyptic adventure will find England's trilogy bold, earnest and full of incident.
dawn:
Harriet A. Adams published Dawn in Boston in 1868, a novel of marriage and spiritual growth. Evidence credits the book to Mrs. Adams, and the title page prints her full name. Hugh and his wife sit in twilight, three years into a harmonious union. Their talk opens the book's question: why are so few marriages harmonious?

Hugh argues that people are married only fractionally, knowing neither themselves nor each other. He would destroy false conditions, not the marriage covenant itself. The novel follows couples whose unions test his doctrine of spiritual assimilation. Adams wrote in the Swedenborgian and reform circles of her day. Dawn treats marriage as a school for souls, where the weak and strong are coupled so that both may grow toward the light her title promises.
four-months-in-a-sneak-box-a-boat-voyage:
Four Months in a Sneak-Box, by Nathaniel H Bishop, recounts a small boat voyage of twenty six hundred miles down the Ohio and Mississippi rivers and along the Gulf of Mexico. Bishop, who had already written up a paper canoe journey from Quebec to the Gulf, dedicates this companion volume to the officers of the United States lighthouse service. Their honest work, he says, taught him respect.

A sneak-box is a low, flat hunting boat, decked over and easy to hide among reeds, and Bishop travels in one for four months. Chapters follow the rivers south through towns, landings, and wild shores, then along the Gulf coast. He writes as a working traveler: weather, currents, food, and the people met at each stop. The introduction presents the book as a sequel written because the first voyage found kind readers on both sides of the Atlantic.
god-the-known-and-god-the-unknown:
Samuel Butler asked what can actually be known about God in God the Known and God the Unknown, first printed as articles in the Examiner in 1879. Butler, fresh from his books on evolution and habit, argues that mankind avoids its largest questions by declaring them settled. He proposes that the God men can know is bound up with life itself, a living unity embracing all living things, while beyond that knowledge a greater unknown remains.

The editor's note explains that Butler revised the articles but never republished them, and follows the revised text. Butler writes theology with a biologist's tools and a satirist's tongue. Readers who know Erewhon or The Way of All Flesh will recognize the mind: devout in curiosity, heretical in conclusions.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin built their partnership through long talks, phone calls, and letters during the 1990s. Briefing Book number 640 gathers the Clinton Presidential Library's released memcons and telcons. Edited by Svetlana Savranskaya and Mary Sarotte, it was published in October 2018. Memcons and telcons are the written records of those meetings and calls.

Quoted lines show Yeltsin promising to build the partnership on their friendship, for the sake of world peace, and Clinton's advice being taken because it had never failed them before. William Burr added notes that set each talk in context. The result lets readers hear two leaders manage nuclear arms, war in Europe, and money troubles in a tone far warmer than public statements of the time.
in-search-of-the-unknown:
Robert W. Chambers published In Search of the Unknown in New York in 1904. He dedicated it to E. Le Grand Beers, a friend drawn to nature study. Chambers jokes that tree-toads, mud-turtles, and fresh-water lobsters led him to write it. The tone is playful from the first page.

Tales follow a narrator who hunts strange beasts and lost kinds. In one scene he pokes through boxes while a dog sleeps, deaf to praise. A pink shirt-waist glimmers through trees as a comic landmark. Science and fancy mix in these linked stories of the unknown.
raabe-the-imperial-crown:
Germany's imperial past supplies the setting for Wilhelm Raabe's historical novel The Imperial Crown, presented here in English. Plain, everyday people carry the story while emperors and their crowns loom in the background. Raabe braids private lives into the grand tale of the nation, as he loved to do.

Deep book-learning joins a warm, humane humor in the telling, so the past never feels like a museum. Men and women who might live on any street bring dead centuries back to life. Raabe believed history happens to ordinary households first of all. English readers meet here the storyteller from Brunswick in his historical vein. The novel rewards patience with steady, accumulating warmth.
shakespeare-bacon-and-the-great-unknown:
Andrew Lang left this book in type at his death, and his widow gave it to the world through Longmans in 1912. Eight pictures light the volume, which Lang inscribed to Horace Howard Furness. A Mr. Bartram checked the quotes and dates with great care after Lang's death.

Lang takes up the long quarrel over who wrote Shakespeare's plays: the Stratford man, Francis Bacon, or some great unknown. His widow asks readers who differ to recall the sad facts of the book's birth. The work stands as a famed scholar's last word on a dispute that still draws heat.
some-persons-unknown: E. W. Hornung wrote Some Persons Unknown, printed at New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1898, under a copyright of the same year. The opening pages list his other books: A Bride from the Bush, The Rogue's March, Irralie's Bushranger, My Lord Duke, and Young Blood.
