The Trow Directory Printing and Bookbinding Company of New York made the book.
stories-of-a-western-town:
Octave Thanet's Stories of a Western Town collects The Besetment of Kurt Lieders, The Face of Failure, Tommy and Thomas, Mother Emeritus, An Assisted Providence, and Harry Lossing. The tales share one small town and its web of neighbors, debts, and kindnesses.

The first tale opens on a December morning at six, with silver rime down the street and dead leaves on the wooden sidewalk. A stout woman in a blue calico gown runs weeping from the tall corner house to a little yellow house, wringing her hands. Thanet writes close, kind studies of German and American townsfolk facing trouble together.
sunshine-sketches-of-a-little-town:
Stephen Leacock's Sunshine Sketches of a Little Town is a set of comic sketches of Mariposa, a small Canadian town, and its hostelry keeper, barber, clergyman, and bank folk. The contents move from The Hostelry of Mr. Smith through The Speculations of Jefferson Thorpe to The Mariposa Bank Mystery and The Great Election in Missinaba County.

Leacock's preface introduces himself with mock modesty. He was born at Swanmoor in Hampshire on December 30, 1869. He migrated to Canada in 1876 because his parents did. His father farmed near Lake Simcoe through hard times. The sketches share that dry voice, laughing at small-town boasting, church socials, whirlwind political campaigns, and fore-ordained love affairs without cruelty.
tales-of-chinatown:
Sax Rohmer published Tales of Chinatown in 1916, gathering ten crime stories set in and around London's Chinatown district. Titles in the contents include The Daughter of Huang Chow, Kerry's Kid, The House of Golden Joss, and The Key of the Temple of Heaven.

The first story opens in a saloon bar near the edge of Chinatown, where a rough ex-prizefighter talks with a sharp, well dressed man known as Diamond Fred. Talk of lying low and hidden news sets a tense, secret mood. Readers get short tales built on mystery, danger, and the pull of an unknown underworld.
tales-of-trail-and-town:
Bret Harte's Tales of Trail and Town turns again to the West, with seven tales that range from mining camps to small towns. Named pieces include The Ancestors of Peter Atherly, The Judgment of Bolinas Plain, and The Youngest Prospector in Calaveras.

The Ancestors of Peter Atherly opens in Rough and Ready, a camp changed by the rich Eureka lead find. Gamblers and bar men poured in, then a church and school rose, yet locks and loans came too. Harte weighs old trust against new greed, as a raw camp hardens into a town and loses the rough faith of its first years.
the-astonishing-history-of-troy-town:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch gives this small volume to Charles Cannan in a letter that opens a 1914 reprint. He tells of a famed teacher and an old pupil. The pupil walked many weary miles to thank him. But for the master's discipline, kept as a boy and recalled as a man, he said, he would never have won the ticket-of-leave he flourished.

Quiller-Couch brings his book in the same spirit, as a child of Cannan's urging. The child, he warns, may stagger its parent, and Cannan may cry out over these pages like the old lady in the ballad. Still, the tale of Troy Town must bear his friend's marks, since a hundred kindnesses helped it grow.
the-blood-red-dawn:
Charles Caldwell Dobie published a novel in 1920 and dedicated it to his mother. Book one opens in the Second Presbyterian Church of San Francisco, where Claire Robson leans forward to ask her mother a speaker's name. Her mother dismisses him as a foreigner of some sort.

The man speaks for Serbia at a Red Cross concert, with America in the war and a draft speeding up. The audience, bored and drawn by coffee from the church kitchen, barely listens. Claire alone feels his inner fire and a strange embarrassment for him. When his eyes turn toward her, that unease sharpens into something personal.
the-camp-fire-girls-at-camp-keewaydin-or:
Hildegard G. Frey wrote The Camp Fire Girls at Camp Keewaydin. Chapter I, On the Way, opens with Captain MacLaren's hoarse all-aboard booming like a fog horn among the cliffs. Seventy-five girls on the dock skurry at once for the Carribou's gangplank. Agony strains forward on the suitcase she helps Hinpoha carry down the hill, and owns the race is hopeless.

Hinpoha, breathless from the scramble off the train, lags farther behind with each step. She will not run down the hill and go sprawling. Sahwah and Oh-Pshaw are on the boat already, and Gladys and Migwan are just getting on. Then the laugh goes up: Katherine's suitcase has come open on the dock, and all her things are spilled out. Hinpoha knows that case well: she sat on it with all her might to shut it, and it will take ten minutes to close again.
the-child-of-the-dawn:
Arthur Christopher Benson, Fellow of Magdalene College, Cambridge, wrote this tale, dated 1912 on its title page. He dedicates it to Herbert Francis William Tatham, in love and hope. A Greek motto stands at its head, and the narrator begins at the end of his former life.

The opening finds the narrator waking after an operation, in deadly sickness and confusion of thought. The trim, bare room, the white bed, and a figure or two swim through pain that fills all his senses at once. His wandering brain turns that pain into a tower of stone, high and blank, with a small sinister window from which something is waved over the rooftops. Then the tower vanishes in a moment. Benson builds a story of death and renewal from that threshold state, in his known reflective manner.
the-circus-comes-to-town: Lebbeus Mitchell, author of One Boy Too Many, wrote this boys' story, copyrighted in 1921 by Little, Brown, and Company and published by Cupples and Leon of New York. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. A frontispiece line shows Jerry keeping fascinated eyes on a chalky white face. The first chapters are titled Ask Your Mother for Fifty Cents, The Black Half-Dollar, and The Width of an Elephant's Tail. No chapter text follows.
the-desert-and-the-sown: Mary Hallock Foote's The Desert and the Sown is shown here only through its contents, which list twenty chapters. The titles move from A Council of the Elders and Introducing a Son-in-Law through Disinherited, A Hunter's Diary, The White Peril, and A Bridegroom of Snow. The Hidden Trail, The Star in the East, Pilgrims and Strangers, and A Station in the Desert. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-evolution-of-an-english-town:
Gordon Home's The Evolution of an English Town tells the story of Pickering in Yorkshire from prehistoric times to the year 1905. Contents move age by age. First comes the vale in the lesser ice age, and its first dwellers. Then the Roman hold, from 55 BC to AD 418. Saxon times run to 1066. Norman times and the Plantagenet years follow.

Home, an artist and antiquary, mixes earthworks, castles, churches, and trades. Each age leaves a mark on one small town's streets. The book shows how deep time sits in a plain market town, layer on layer.
the-gray-dawn: Stewart Edward White wrote The Gray Dawn. Pictures are by Thomas Fogarty. Only front matter is present here. It gives a list of White's other books and a list of principal characters. The book list names The Blazed Trail, Arizona Nights, and The Rules of the Game. The character list names Milton Keith, a young lawyer from Baltimore, and his wife Nan. It names John Sherwood, a gambler, and Arthur Morrell, an English adventurer. It names James King of William, a modern crusader. No chapter text is present.
the-green-satin-gown: Laura E. Richards wrote The Green Satin Gown. Etheldred B. Barry made the pictures. The book was published in May 1903. It is dedicated to the girls of the Friday Club of Gardiner, Maine. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, the dedication, and a contents list. The tales named are the title tale and Blue Egyptians. They are Little Benjamin, Don Alonzo, and The Shed Chamber. They are Maine to the Rescue and The Scarlet Leaves. No tale text is present.
the-honorable-miss-a-story-of-an-old-fas: L. T. Meade wrote The Honorable Miss, subtitled a story of an old-fashioned town, with a heading in the record dated 1890. Meade is named as the author of The Young Mutineer, World of Girls, A Very Naughty Girl, and Sweet Girl Graduate. The pages present add a publisher's list for the L. T. Meade series from Hurst & Company of New York, naming Bunch of Cherries, Daddy's Girl, and Dr. Rumsey's Patient among its volumes. Only the title page and series list are present here.
the-innocence-of-father-brown:
G. K. Chesterton's first Father Brown collection holds twelve stories. The Blue Cross leads the list. The Secret Garden and The Queer Feet follow. The Flying Stars and The Invisible Man appear. The Three Tools of Death closes the set. The Blue Cross opens at Harwich. A boat lets loose a swarm of folk. One man wears a pale grey jacket and a straw hat. His lean face ends in a curt black beard. Nothing shows what his clothes conceal.

His waistcoat covers a police card. His hat covers a first-rate mind. He is Valentin, head of the Paris police. He has come from Brussels to make a famous arrest. The great criminal Flambeau is in England. Police of three countries tracked him from Ghent onward. Chesterton puts the famed detective on stage first. His small priest catches up quietly. Father Brown's innocence works as a method.
the-jealousies-of-a-country-town:
Balzac's Les Rivalités returns to its collected form here. Two existing translations are joined in one volume. Katharine Prescott Wormeley rendered An Old Maid. Ellen Marriage rendered The Collection of Antiquities. George Saintsbury supplied the introduction. He argues the two Alençon stories connect closely. The Chevalier de Valois figures notably in each. Both study the old noblesse of one town.

Saintsbury calls An Old Maid among Balzac's best and liveliest works. Its opening picture of the Chevalier is a classic, he says. The portrait of country-town society is nearly perfect. His one reservation is the sentimental Athanase. He compares Athanase unfavorably with Dickens's Augustus Moddle. The volume shows provincial France clearly. A fading aristocracy fights its jealousies in drawing rooms.
the-mystery-of-mr-bernard-brown:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's The Mystery of Mr. Bernard Brown, dated 1896 and subtitled Or, The New Tenant, is present here only in title page and a bare contents list, so the mystery does not appear. Twenty chapters are listed, numbered from I to XX in Roman numerals, and not one carries a title.

Those twenty blank headings are the entire showing. No character speaks, no tenant arrives, and no opening sentence of Oppenheim's novel is included. The record gives only the frame: an early Oppenheim mystery from 1896, and a subtitle promising a new tenant. Its story divides into twenty untitled chapters. Their contents remain hidden behind the numbers.
the-nine-unknown:
Only the Project Gutenberg Australia header for The Nine Unknown is present here, so Talbot Mundy's novel itself does not appear. The header dates the book 1923, names Mundy as author, and gives the electronic text number 0900641. Colin Choat produced it from page images supplied by Tejaswy Appalla, with corrections in 2010 by Bob Barnett; it was first posted in August 2009 and last updated in January 2010.

Advertising script from the source site is embedded in the header, a defect of the wrapper rather than the book. Production notes begin at the foot of the pages shown, and no title page, contents, or line of Mundy's adventure is included in what is present.
the-puppet-crown: Harold MacGrath's novel runs to twenty-nine chapters. The list opens with a scepter that was a stick. It moves through a coup and a red chateau to a court fete. A final chapter rests in still waters. A dedication honors the author's father. A verse from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam stands before chapter one. Only the title pages and full contents list are present here. The story itself does not appear on these pages.
the-story-of-a-calico-clown:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Make Believe story in ten chapters. She also wrote the Bobbsey Twins and Bunny Brown series. The tale follows a toy clown. He suffers a broken leg. He dances, takes a trip down town, and joins a toy party. Chapter one, The Giant's Swing, opens on a toy counter in a big department store.

The Elephant from the Noah's Ark makes a promise. He tells the Double Humped Camel in the next stall of a most wonderful time that night. The Camel stands by a drum. He looks toward a Jack in the Box. He asks what kind of time it will be. Hope's premise, that department-store toys talk and adventure after dark, carries the whole series of these little books.
the-story-of-bawn: Katharine Tynan, author of The Dear Irish Girl, published this novel with A. C. McClurg and Company in Chicago in 1907. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents list twenty-four chapters. They move from Myself and The Ghosts onward. Richard Dawson, a rough lover, and a trap follow. Flight and a crying in the night come next. The blow falling closes the list. Bawn's story itself does not appear.
the-story-of-cooperstown: Ralph Birdsall, rector of Christ Church, wrote this history of Cooperstown, New York, published by Charles Scribner's Sons with sixty-eight illustrations from photographs. Only the title pages and the head of a contents list are present here. This printing is dated 1925. It follows a copyright of 1917 and three earlier printings. Birdsall's account of the village itself does not appear.
the-wisdom-of-father-brown:
G. K. Chesterton's The Wisdom of Father Brown gathers twelve detective stories about a Catholic priest who solves crimes. Titles in the contents include The Paradise of Thieves and The Purple Wig. The opening story, The Absence of Mr Glass, begins in Scarborough. There the criminologist Dr. Orion Hood keeps consulting rooms facing the North Sea.

Hood's rooms are luxurious yet ruled by strict tidiness. Cigars sit ranked by strength on a special table. Chesterton uses such ordered settings to set up disorderly crimes. Father Brown's quiet reasoning then cuts through them. Readers who enjoy puzzle mysteries with a moral edge will find plenty here.
wild-animals-i-have-known:
Ernest Thompson Seton wrote Wild Animals I Have Known, a set of animal life stories. The tales name Lobo, king of Currumpaw, Silverspot the crow, and Raggylug the cottontail rabbit. Seton's own dog Bingo and a pacing mustang also star. In a note, Seton insists the stories are true in the main. The animals were real, he says, with strong character of their own.

Seton argues that nature writing loses much by vague general treatment. One full animal life teaches more than a sketch of a whole kind, he holds. Some figures are pieced from records, which he grants, but Lobo and Bingo stand near exact. Readers meet wild lives told as biography, with heroism in fang and feather.
with-links-of-steel-or-the-peril-of-the-: Nothing past the title page and chapter list is present here for Nicholas Carter's With Links of Steel, a Nick Carter detective tale, so the story does not start. Street and Smith printed it in New York in 1904 as New Magnet Library number 1164. The contents open with a crafty robbery. A diamond gang, a shot in the dark, and a man found dead follow. Nick strikes a startling clue at chapter nine. The diamond plant, cross-purposes, and a last trick close the list.
